items.title: Home
items.text:
HomeGAP is a self-hosted alternative to Cloudflare Tunnels and WARP. Your homelab is the only origin, and nothing at home accepts inbound connections. Regional VPS nodes take each viewer's connection near the viewer and send it home through a private WireGuard mesh that the homelab dials out.

One orchestrator container on the homelab controls the system from Docker labels:

  • Regional nodes are Ubuntu VPS servers from any provider, in any location. Each node runs Traefik, a maintenance page and the agent of HomeGAP.
  • Bunny DNS sends each viewer to the nearest healthy node. Health checks remove a node that fails.
  • The orchestrator reads the labels and writes the routes of every node, the mesh between the nodes and the homelab, and the DNS records. It also installs and maintains the nodes over SSH.

Caution

HomeGAP is early-stage software. Test it on a domain that nothing depends on, for example a spare domain or a subdomain delegated to Bunny DNS. Then move production traffic to it.

items.title: Home
items.text:
Publish homelab services worldwide through your own regional edge nodes. No inbound ports, no third-party tunnel.

Getting started · How it works · Label reference

items.title: Features
items.text:
• The origin stays hidden. The homelab has no open ports. The homelab dials out to each node.
  • End-to-end TLS by default. Nodes route by the TLS server name and never see plaintext. One label moves TLS termination to the nodes. See Traffic paths.
  • HTTP(S), raw TCP and UDP, and private services that only the devices of the VPN can reach. See Services.
  • Geo routing with failover. Each viewer reaches the nearest healthy node. See DNS routing and health checks.
  • A VPN with its own sign-in. The Pangolin apps and olm connect to the sign-in of HomeGAP, with a HomeGAP password or an OpenID Connect provider such as Authelia. Roles decide which private services a device can reach. See Sign-in and VPN.
  • Exits through a node or through the homelab. A device can send all its traffic to the internet through an exit. When the homelab is down, the exits through a node continue to work. See Exits and tunnel DNS.
  • Real client addresses. With the PROXY protocol, the homelab sees the address of each viewer. See Client addresses.
  • One label publishes a service. Docker labels are the source of truth. The orchestrator makes the rest match them.
  • Node lifecycle from a bare VPS. A dashboard wizard turns a fresh server into a node over SSH. Updates roll out one node at a time, with automatic rollback. See Add a node.
  • A built-in dashboard for health, pausing, re-provisioning, users and devices, speed tests, diagnostics and node management. It also serves this documentation for its own version. See The dashboard.
  • Self-hosted maps of the nodes and the homelab, on the dashboard and on an optional public status page. No third-party map service. See Maps and locations.
  • The orchestrator is never in the traffic path. If it stops, the nodes continue to serve, the mesh stays up and DNS continues to resolve.

Start with Getting started. For the model behind the system, read How HomeGAP works.

These pages are the documentation for HomeGAP version dev.

items.title: License
items.text: HomeGAP has the MIT license.

items.title: Configuration
items.text: HomeGAP reads its configuration from one YAML file. This page tells you where the file is, when changes apply and how HomeGAP checks the file.

items.title: The file
items.text:
The orchestrator finds the file in this order:

  1. The --config PATH option.
  2. The HOMEGAP_CONFIG environment variable.
  3. The default path, /config/config.yml.

With the shipped stack, the file is config/config.yml in the folder of the stack. homegap init writes a first version with the settings that most homelabs need. The file config/config.example.yml in the same folder shows more keys. For every key, see the Configuration reference.

The parser is strict. An unknown key is an error, and the orchestrator does not start.

The file holds no secret. See Secrets.

items.title: A minimal config
items.text:
domain: example.net
bunny:
  zone: example.net
acme:
  email: ops@example.net
nodes: []
dashboard:
  bind: 0.0.0.0:8088

items.title: When changes apply
items.text:
The orchestrator reads the file again on each pass. Thus most edits apply without a restart. If an edit is not valid, the orchestrator writes the error to the log, and the last good configuration stays in effect.

These changes need a restart of the orchestrator:

  • The first activation of the speed test (speedtest.enabled) or the status page (status_page.enabled), if neither was on at the start. The two share one listener, which starts only with the orchestrator.
  • A change of speedtest.bind.
  • A change of the dashboard token. The orchestrator reads the token one time, at the start.
  • A change of dashboard.bind.
  • A change of data_dir.

The homegap-sign-in container reads the sign_in and vpn parts of the file one time, at its start. After a change of these parts, start the container again:

docker compose restart homegap-sign-in

items.title: Check the file
items.text:
To check the file, run homegap validate. In the container, use this command:

docker compose exec orchestrator homegap validate

To check a different file, add --config PATH. If the file is valid, the command prints OK: <n> node(s), domain <domain>, zone <zone>. If not, it prints Invalid configuration: and the list of errors.

items.title: Edits from the dashboard
items.text:
With dashboard.allow_config_edits: true (the default), the dashboard can add and remove nodes, and set the location of a node and of the homelab. Each such change writes the config file again. The config mount must be writable for this.

Each change from the dashboard starts from the file on the disk. Thus an edit that you make by hand a moment before stays in the file. If the file has an error, HomeGAP does not write it, and the dashboard shows the error.

Before each write, HomeGAP saves the previous file next to it as <file>.bak-<epoch ms>, with mode 0600. It keeps the newest 10 backups. The new file starts with this comment:

# Managed by HomeGAP; edited from the dashboard. Previous version saved alongside as .bak-*

Caution

The new file contains only the values that are different from the defaults. If you edit nodes on the dashboard, HomeGAP does not keep the comments of your file. Keep a copy of your commented file if you need it.

items.title: Durations
items.text: A duration is a number with a unit: ms, s, m or h. A number without a unit is in seconds. Examples are 60s, 5m and 2h.

items.title: Validation rules
items.text:
homegap validate and each read of the file check these rules.

The domains and Bunny:

  • domain is a plain hostname, without a leading dot and without *.
  • bunny.zone is equal to domain, or a parent of it.
  • bunny.routing is geolocation, latency or none.
  • bunny.monitor is http, ping or none.
  • Each domain of extra_domains is a plain hostname in lower case.
  • The zone of each extra domain is equal to that domain, or a parent of it.
  • No extra domain is inside domain or a different extra domain, and none contains one of them.

The certificate:

  • acme.directory starts with https://.
  • With acme.caa: true, acme.caa_issuer is a domain name.

The nodes:

  • Each node id matches ^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,30}$, and each node id is unique.
  • host is a hostname or an IP address.
  • ssh_user matches ^[a-z_][a-z0-9_-]{0,31}$.
  • ssh_port is from 1 to 65535.
  • ssh_key_file is not empty.
  • management_host, if you set it, is a hostname.
  • public_ipv4 and public_ipv6 are IP addresses.
  • Each ssh_allow_from entry is an IP address or a CIDR.
  • Each node has an IPv4 address (public_ipv4, or a host that is an IPv4 literal), or a public_ipv6.
  • With geolocation routing, each node has a location or a known region code.
  • With latency routing, each node has a latency_zone.

The reconcile loop:

  • reconcile.resync_interval is 1s or more.
  • Each other key of reconcile that is a duration has a valid value.

The mesh:

  • mesh.subnet is a valid IPv4 subnet. It does not overlap 100.64.0.0/10, where the VPN has its addresses.
  • mesh.subnet has space for 32 nodes (/26 or larger).
  • mesh.port is from 1 to 65535.

The sign-in and the VPN:

  • sign_in.url starts with https://.
  • With sign_in.passwords: false, sign_in.oidc is set.
  • sign_in.oidc needs sign_in.url.
  • sign_in.oidc.issuer starts with https://.
  • sign_in.oidc.client_id is not empty.
  • sign_in.oidc.scopes contains openid.
  • Each entry of vpn.tunnel_dns.resolvers is an IP address.
  • vpn.port, the port after it, vpn.exit_port and the port after it are four different ports from 1 to 65535.
  • vpn.client_subnet is a /16.

The dashboard:

  • dashboard.bind is in the form host:port.
  • dashboard.hostname, if you set it, is a single lowercase label that matches ^[a-z][a-z0-9]{0,20}$.
  • With dashboard.hostname, dashboard.access is private or public.
  • dashboard.hostname is different from the hostname of the speed test and of the status page, if they are enabled.
  • dashboard.sso needs dashboard.hostname.
  • dashboard.sso.middleware is a Traefik middleware with its provider, for example authelia@docker.
  • dashboard.sso.user_header and dashboard.sso.groups_header are header names.
  • No group of dashboard.sso.groups and dashboard.sso.read_only_groups is empty or contains a comma.

When homelab.ssh.enabled is true:

  • homelab.ssh.hostname is a single lowercase label.
  • homelab.ssh.port is from 1 to 65535.

When the status page is enabled:

  • status_page.hostname is a single lowercase label.
  • status_page.hostname is different from speedtest.hostname, if the speed test is also enabled.
  • status_page.title has 60 characters or fewer.
  • speedtest.bind is in the form host:port, and it is different from dashboard.bind.

When the speed test is enabled:

  • speedtest.hostname is a single lowercase label.
  • speedtest.phase_seconds is from 2 to 30.
  • speedtest.link_budget_gb is from 1 to 1000.
  • speedtest.streams is from 1 to 16.
  • speedtest.link_ttl is a valid duration, and speedtest.bind is in the form host:port.
  • speedtest.bind is different from dashboard.bind.

items.title: Certificates
items.text: A node holds a certificate only for a name that it terminates. This page tells you which names those are, how HomeGAP orders the certificate, and why a node cannot get other certificates.

items.title: The risk of a certificate on a node
items.text:
A browser accepts each valid certificate for a name. All traffic to your domain goes through a node. Thus a person with root on a node can read the traffic of each name on the certificate of that node. That person ends TLS on the node, reads or changes the request, and sends the request to the homelab. The browser and the homelab see no difference.

For this reason, HomeGAP gives a node no certificate for a passthrough name. The Traefik of your homelab holds the certificate of a passthrough name, and HomeGAP does not order or renew it.

items.title: Which names are on the certificate
items.text:
Name On the certificate of the nodes The management name of each node, node-<id>.<domain>. Yes. The name of the sign-in, from sign_in.url. Yes. The shared names of the status page and the speed test. Yes. A service with homegap.tls: terminate. Yes. A service with homegap.tls: passthrough. No. The front door with passthrough, with or without homegap.wildcard. No. The front door with terminate. Yes: the root name, and the names of the status page and the speed test for each node. With homegap.wildcard, *.<domain> is on the certificate, and it replaces each name one label under the domain.

A service that speaks plain HTTP is always in terminate mode. See Traffic paths.

The activity log shows each order, with the number of names. An order can take some minutes, because it waits for DNS. The reconcile pass does not wait for the order. When the order is complete, the next pass gives the new certificate to the nodes.

items.title: The front door in terminate mode with a wildcard
items.text:
This is the only setup that puts a wildcard certificate on the nodes. The nodes then end TLS for each name one label under your domain. A person with root on a node can read all of that traffic.

Warning

With homegap.tls: terminate and homegap.wildcard: "true" on the front door, the nodes hold a certificate for *.<domain>. Use this setup only if you trust each node and its provider with all web traffic of the domain.

In this setup, HomeGAP refuses a service with homegap.tls: passthrough on a hostname one label under the domain. The wildcard on the nodes covers that hostname, so passthrough protects nothing. The error is homegap.tls=passthrough is refused for <hostname>. Set homegap.tls: terminate on that service, or use passthrough on the front door.

HomeGAP does not refuse a raw TCP or UDP service. A certificate has no effect on a protocol that does not use TLS. But a raw TCP service that uses TLS for a name under the domain has the same risk as a web service.

items.title: How HomeGAP orders the certificate
items.text:
The orchestrator on the homelab orders one certificate from Let's Encrypt. The certificate lists each name from the table above. Each node gets the same certificate and the same key.

HomeGAP uses the DNS challenge:

  1. The orchestrator starts Lego, an ACME client in the homegap image.
  2. For each name, Lego asks the orchestrator for a TXT record _acme-challenge.<name>. Lego calls an endpoint on the loopback address of the orchestrator.
  3. The orchestrator writes the record with its own Bunny client. Lego never gets the Bunny key.
  4. Let's Encrypt reads the records and issues the certificate.
  5. The orchestrator removes the records and sends the certificate to each node.

A node orders no certificate. The Traefik on a node has no certificate resolver, and a node has no DNS key.

HomeGAP orders a new certificate, with a new key, in these cases:

  • The list of names changes.
  • One third of the lifetime of the certificate remains.
  • The ACME directory in the config changes.

If a name leaves the list, HomeGAP also revokes the old certificate, because the nodes have its key. This occurs when you remove a node, or when you change a service from terminate to passthrough. HomeGAP revokes the old certificate only after the new order succeeds. It does not revoke the old certificate if the ACME directory changed in the same order.

A new certificate does not restart the stack of a node. HomeGAP writes the new files, and Traefik loads them.

One certificate has at most 100 names. With more names, the order fails, and the activity log shows the error.

In dry run, or while changes are paused, HomeGAP orders no certificate. The Config page shows the order as a pending change.

items.title: The CAA records
items.text:
HomeGAP publishes two CAA records for domain and for each extra domain, with the tags issue and issuewild. Each has this value:

letsencrypt.org; validationmethods=dns-01

With these records, only Let's Encrypt can issue a certificate for the domain, and only with the DNS challenge. A node has no DNS key. Thus a compromised node cannot order a certificate for one of your names, although the traffic for that name goes through it.

HomeGAP removes each other CAA record at domain, because it can give more permissions.

Caution

The CAA records also apply to the Traefik of your homelab. It must order its certificates from Let's Encrypt with the DNS challenge. If it uses a different certificate authority or a different challenge, its renewals fail. In that case, set acme.caa: false, or set acme.caa_issuer to the CAA name of your certificate authority.

To publish no CAA records for one extra domain, set caa: false on that domain.

items.title: Config
items.text:
acme:
  email: ops@example.net
Key Default What it does email admin@<domain> The contact address of the ACME account. staging false Uses the staging directory of Let's Encrypt. Browsers do not trust its certificates. Use it for tests. directory The directory of Let's Encrypt. The address of a different ACME directory. It must start with https://. caa true Publishes the CAA records. caa_issuer letsencrypt.org The certificate authority in the CAA records.

items.title: Where HomeGAP keeps the certificate
items.text:
The ACME account key, the certificate and its key are in acme/ in the data directory of the orchestrator. Each file has mode 0600. Include this folder in your backup of the data directory. If you lose it, HomeGAP makes a new account and orders a new certificate.

On a node, the certificate is config/traefik/certs/homegap.crt and the key is homegap.key, with mode 0600. The file config/traefik/dynamic/homegap-tls.yml tells Traefik where they are.

items.title: The Certificates page
items.text:
The dashboard has a Certificates tab on the DNS page. It shows state only. It never shows a key, a certificate file, the ACME account key or a challenge value. It has no control to upload or download a certificate.

The page has these parts:

  • The status line gives the state in one sentence: valid, an order that runs, a failed order, the renewal window, or no certificate.
  • Node certificate shows the lifetime with the issue date, the renewal date and the expiry, and each name on the certificate. If the names in the config differ from the names on the certificate, it shows the names to add and to remove.
  • Delivery to the nodes shows, for each node, the version of the certificate that it has and what it serves on its management name.
  • What a visitor gets shows a TLS probe of each public name through each node. A name in passthrough mode has the tag Homelab: the Traefik of the homelab holds its certificate.
  • Orders shows the last 20 orders and revocations, with the reason, the result and the duration.
  • Who can issue shows the CAA records that HomeGAP publishes, and the CAA records that DNS has now.

The page has four actions:

Action What it does Order now Starts the order in the next pass, without the wait of one hour after a failure. HomeGAP refuses it after 5 failed orders in one hour. Send again Writes the certificate files on the node again in the next pass. Check now Runs the TLS probes again. Replace the key Orders a new certificate with a new key for the same names, and revokes the old certificate. Use it when you think that a person has the key of a node.

A new node waits for an order with its management name. Until then, it answers that name with the default certificate of Traefik. The dashboard shows the node as "waiting for certificate", not as down.

items.title: Expiry and failures
items.text:
If an order fails, the nodes keep the certificate that they have. HomeGAP keeps the state of the order in the data directory, writes a short cause in the activity log, and tries again after one hour. The full error text of the ACME client is in the detail of the log entry. A node without a certificate answers its names with the default certificate of Traefik, and browsers show a warning.

The Certificates page shows the cause of a failed order:

Cause What to do DNS did not show the challenge record in time. Bunny DNS was slow. HomeGAP tries again after one hour. Let's Encrypt refused: too many orders. Let's Encrypt accepts 5 failed orders for each name in one hour. Wait for the next hour. A CAA record forbids the order. A CAA record that HomeGAP does not manage, on a name above domain, refuses Let's Encrypt. Remove it or change it. The Bunny key is missing or refused. Set the Bunny API key, and make sure that it can change the zone. The ACME service did not answer. The homelab cannot reach Let's Encrypt. Check the internet connection of the homelab. More than 100 names. One certificate holds at most 100 names. Use a front door in terminate mode with a wildcard, or change services to passthrough.

items.title: DNS routing and health checks
items.text: Bunny DNS sends each viewer to a healthy node. This page tells you how to configure the routing and the monitors, which records HomeGAP creates and how failover works.

items.title: Routing
items.text:
bunny.routing selects how Bunny chooses a node:

Value How Bunny chooses geolocation (default) By the location (latitude and longitude) of each node. If a node has only a region, HomeGAP uses the center of the region. latency By the Bunny latency zones. Each node needs a latency_zone. none No smart routing. The records are plain records.

bunny.ttl sets the TTL of the A and AAAA records (default 60 seconds). The CAA records always have a TTL of 3600 seconds.

items.title: Record sets and records of one node
items.text:
HomeGAP creates two types of records.

A record set is for a name that more than one node serves. It has one A record for each node, and one AAAA record for each node with public_ipv6. Each record has the routing of bunny.routing and the monitor of bunny.monitor. Bunny sends a viewer to one member of the set.

A record of one node is for a name that only that node serves, for example its management name. It has no routing and no monitor.

items.title: Monitors
items.text:
bunny.monitor sets the monitor on each record of a record set:

  • http (the default, and we recommend it). Bunny sends a request to http://<node-ip>/. The answer shows that the path from the node to the homelab works.
  • ping. Bunny sends a ping to the node. The answer shows only that the node is up.
  • none. Bunny does no check, and a failed node stays in the answers.

With http, the Traefik of the node answers the request on port 80 at the IP address of the node. It sends the request over the mesh to one service of the homelab, with the health path of that service. That service is the front door. On a node that does not serve the front door, it is the first HTTP service of that node. The health path is the homegap.healthcheck label of the service (default /).

If the service does not answer, the node answers 502, and Bunny shows the node as offline. A node with no HTTP service always answers 502. Thus, with the http monitor, Bunny shows such a node as offline.

items.title: Failover
items.text:
Bunny removes the offline members from a record set. A different node then answers. If all members are offline, Bunny returns all of them.

A resolver keeps an answer for the TTL (bunny.ttl). Thus some viewers go to the failed node for that time after Bunny removes it.

Note

A single record cannot fail over. With one node, Bunny continues to answer with that node when it is down.

items.title: The records
items.text:
Name Purpose Type of record <domain> root A record set with each node that serves the front door. *.<domain> wildcard A record set, only with homegap.wildcard on the front door. Each public hostname of a service service:<key> One record set for each hostname, also when several raw services share it. The key is the key of the first service. The name of the sign-in, from sign_in.url service:<key> A record set. The sign-in is a public service of HomeGAP itself. speedtest.<domain> speedtest A record set, only without a wildcard. With a wildcard, the wildcard set covers the name. speedtest-<node>.<domain> speedtest A record of one node, for each node that serves the front door. status.<domain> status A record set, also with a wildcard. status-<node>.<domain> status A record of one node, for each node that serves the front door. node-<id>.<domain> management A record of one node, for each node. <domain> caa Two CAA records (issue and issuewild), with acme.caa: true (the default). See Certificates.

The records of the speed test and the status page exist only when a front door exists and the page is enabled.

A record set includes only the nodes that serve the service (homegap.regions). For a shared hostname, it includes every node that serves one of its services.

During a certificate order, HomeGAP also creates TXT records at _acme-challenge names. It removes them after the order.

items.title: A new node and a removed node
items.text:
A new node gets no DNS records until its stack is up. Before that, the node answers nothing, so Bunny must not send a viewer to it. After the first successful provisioning, the next pass creates the records of the node. The CAA records belong to no node, and HomeGAP creates them at once.

When you remove a node from the config, HomeGAP deletes its records in the next pass.

items.title: Ownership of records
items.text:
HomeGAP marks each of its records with the comment managed-by:homegap <purpose> node=<id>. For the CAA records, the id is homelab. The comment of a challenge record is managed-by:homegap acme-challenge. HomeGAP does not touch records that it did not create, except at the names that it manages.

Warning

At a name that HomeGAP manages, HomeGAP deletes some records that it did not create. The log and the diff on the Config page give the reason "collides with a managed record set".

  • HomeGAP deletes an A or AAAA record with the same name and type as a managed record.
  • With acme.caa: true, HomeGAP deletes a CAA record at domain that it did not create.
  • HomeGAP deletes each CNAME record at that name.
  • HomeGAP adopts a record that has exactly the desired value.

Before you disable dry run, look for delete rows in the diff on the Config page.

items.title: Pauses
items.text: HomeGAP does not create, change or delete the records of a paused node or a paused service. You pause a service with the homegap.pause label or from the dashboard. While all changes are paused, HomeGAP changes no record.

items.title: Extra domains
items.text: Each extra domain has its own zone, or shares a zone with a different domain. HomeGAP writes each record to the zone of its domain, with the same routing, monitor and TTL. If one zone fails, HomeGAP still syncs the other zones, and the activity log names the zone that failed.

items.title: Reads of the zone
items.text:
A change to the desired records syncs at once. When the desired records do not change, HomeGAP reads the whole zone again every reconcile.dns_check_interval (default 5 minutes). Thus it finds edits from the Bunny console.

After a change, HomeGAP asks the nameservers of the zone for the record. Until each nameserver has it, the record shows "not on every nameserver", and HomeGAP asks again on each pass.

items.title: The DNS page
items.text: The DNS page on the dashboard shows the records, the state of their monitors and if they match the desired state. To add records of your own, for example a TXT record for a verification, use the Zone records tab of that page. It refuses a record that HomeGAP deletes. See The dashboard.

items.title: Configuration reference
items.text: This page lists every key of the config file, with its type and its default. A key with no default is optional, unless the table says that it is necessary.

items.title: Top level
items.text: Key Type Default What it does project string home-gap The name of the project. domain string None. Necessary. The base domain that HomeGAP serves, for example example.net. extra_domains list [] More domains that services can use. See Extra domains. data_dir string /data The data directory of the orchestrator. reconcile object See below. The reconcile loop. bunny object None. Necessary. Bunny DNS. node_stack object See below. What each node runs. acme object See below. The certificate that HomeGAP orders and sends to the nodes. mesh object See below. The private WireGuard mesh between the homelab and each node. It is always on. sign_in object See below. The sign-in of HomeGAP for the apps. vpn object See below. The VPN of the devices that sign in. agent object See below. The agent of HomeGAP on each node. nodes list [] The nodes. dashboard object See below. The dashboard. speedtest object See below. The speed tests. status_page object See below. The public status page. homelab object See below. The homelab: its location and SSH to its host. map object See below. The map tiles.

items.title: reconcile
items.text: Key Type Default What it does resync_interval duration 60s The interval of the full resync. The minimum is 1s. debounce duration 2s The debounce of Docker events. dry_run boolean false Does discovery and writes the desired state to the log, but makes no changes. node_check_interval duration 5m The interval of the SSH drift check on each node. dns_check_interval duration 5m How often HomeGAP reads the full Bunny zone again when the desired records do not change. A change to the desired records syncs at once. removal_grace duration 3m How long the services of a container stay after the container is gone. See Services.

items.title: extra_domains[]
items.text: Key Type Default What it does domain string None. Necessary. A domain for services, for example example.org. It cannot be inside domain or a different extra domain. zone string The value of domain. The Bunny DNS zone. It is equal to the domain or a parent of it. It uses the API key of bunny. caa boolean true With false, HomeGAP publishes no CAA records for this domain. Use it if the root of the domain has a service that gets its certificate in a different way. It has no effect without acme.caa.

items.title: bunny
items.text:
Key Type Default What it does zone string None. Necessary. The Bunny DNS zone. It is equal to domain or a parent of it. api_key_env string BUNNY_API_KEY The environment variable with the Bunny API key. api_key_file string None. A file with the Bunny API key. ttl integer 60 The TTL of the A and AAAA records, in seconds. The CAA records always have a TTL of 3600. routing string geolocation geolocation, latency or none. monitor string http The monitor on each record of a record set: http, ping or none. api_url string https://api.bunny.net The URL of the Bunny API.

See DNS routing and health checks.

items.title: node_stack
items.text: Key Type Default What it does traefik_image string docker.io/traefik:v3.7.16 The Traefik image. maintenance_image string docker.io/library/python:3.13-alpine The image that runs the maintenance page of a node. The page needs only the standard library of Python. crowdsec_image string docker.io/crowdsecurity/crowdsec:v1.8.2 The CrowdSec image. crowdsec_bouncer_version string v1.4.6 The version of the CrowdSec bouncer of Traefik. install_dir string /opt/homegap The directory of the stack on each node. crowdsec boolean false Enables CrowdSec and its bouncer on the Traefik of each node. crowdsec_fail_closed boolean false With true, a node refuses a request while it cannot reach the AppSec component of CrowdSec. With false, the request goes through. mesh_port_base integer 40000 The start of the range of ports on the mesh address of the homelab. Each service that a node reaches by name gets one. No node publishes them. tcp_tuning boolean true Tunes TCP on each node: BBR congestion control, the fq qdisc, larger socket buffers and MTU probing. The settings are in /etc/sysctl.d/99-homegap.conf.

items.title: acme
items.text:
Key Type Default What it does email string admin@<domain> The contact address of the ACME account. directory string The directory of Let's Encrypt. The address of a different ACME directory. It must start with https://. staging boolean false Uses the staging directory of Let's Encrypt. caa boolean true Publishes CAA records that let only caa_issuer issue certificates, and only with the DNS challenge. caa_issuer string letsencrypt.org The certificate authority in the CAA records.

See Certificates.

items.title: mesh
items.text:
Key Type Default What it does subnet string 10.77.0.0/24 The IPv4 subnet of the mesh addresses. It must not overlap 100.64.0.0/10. Use /26 or larger. port integer 51821 The UDP port of the mesh on each node. The firewall of the node opens it.

See The mesh.

items.title: sign_in
items.text:
Key Type Default What it does url string None. The address of the sign-in, for example https://vpn.example.net. You put it into the apps. Each node serves it. Without it, there is no sign-in and no VPN. passwords boolean true Lets a user sign in with a HomeGAP password. With false, HomeGAP accepts only the provider of oidc. oidc.issuer string None. Necessary with oidc. The address of the OpenID Connect provider. It must start with https://. oidc.client_id string None. Necessary with oidc. The client id of HomeGAP at the provider. oidc.client_secret_env string HOMEGAP_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET The environment variable of the sign-in container that holds the client secret. oidc.name string single sign-on The name on the button of the sign-in page. oidc.scopes list ["openid", "email", "profile"] The scopes that HomeGAP requests. The list must contain openid.

The oidc object is optional. See Sign-in.

items.title: vpn
items.text:
Key Type Default What it does client_subnet string 100.90.0.0/16 The subnet of the device addresses in the tunnel. It must be a /16. The first address is the homelab. utility_subnet string 100.96.128.0/24 The subnet that the apps use for their DNS proxy and for the addresses of private names. port integer 51830 The UDP port of each node that the apps connect to. The node forwards it to the homelab. The next port up is in use inside the tunnel. exit_port integer 51840 The UDP port of each node for the devices that use the node as their exit. The next port up is in use inside the tunnel. endpoint string The name of the sign-in. The name or address that the devices send their WireGuard packets to, for the homelab. It must go to a node. exit_nodes.nodes boolean false Offers "Exit via <node>" for each node. exit_nodes.homelab boolean false Offers "Exit via homelab". exit_nodes.roles list [] The roles that can use the exits. Admin can always use them. tunnel_dns.resolvers list ["8.8.8.8"] The DNS servers that the apps reach through the tunnel, as IP addresses. An empty list disables them. tunnel_dns.roles list ["Member"] The roles that can use these DNS servers. Admin can always use them.

See Exits and tunnel DNS.

items.title: agent
items.text: Key Type Default What it does image string ghcr.io/drewcarlson/homegap:<tag> The HomeGAP image that a node runs as its agent. The default tag is the value of HOMEGAP_VERSION. Without that variable, the tag is the version of the orchestrator. revision string The value of HOMEGAP_REVISION. The build of the image. The image sets HOMEGAP_REVISION to its commit. When the revision changes, each node pulls the image of the agent again. A tag such as main then brings its new build to the nodes.

items.title: nodes[]
items.text:
Key Type Default What it does id string None. Necessary. The node id. It must match ^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,30}$. region string "" A region code: NA, SA, EU, AF, AS, OC or ME. provider string "" The VPS provider, for your information. host string None. Necessary. The SSH address of the node. public_ipv4 string The value of host, if host is an IPv4 literal. The public IPv4 address in DNS. public_ipv6 string None. The public IPv6 address in DNS. os string "" The OS of the node, for example ubuntu-24.04. ssh_user string root The SSH user. ssh_port integer 22 The SSH port. If you change it for a node that HomeGAP manages, HomeGAP moves the SSH server of the node to the new port. See Node updates. ssh_key_file string None. Necessary. The private SSH key, as a path in the orchestrator container. location object None. { latitude, longitude, name }. The name shows on the maps. latency_zone string None. The Bunny latency zone, for latency routing. management_host string node-<id>.<domain> The name of the node itself, which goes only to this node. HomeGAP checks the certificate of the node there. firewall boolean true Lets HomeGAP manage ufw on the node. ssh_allow_from list [] The sources (IP addresses or CIDRs) that can reach SSH. An empty list means anywhere. install_docker boolean true Installs Docker Engine if it is not on the node.

Warning

If you set ssh_allow_from and the public IP address of the orchestrator leaves the list, the orchestrator cannot connect to the node. Then correct the rule from the console of the provider.

If a node has a region but no location, HomeGAP uses a rough center of the region:

Region Latitude Longitude NA 39.8 -98.6 SA -15.6 -56.1 EU 50.1 8.7 AF 1.7 17.3 ME 25.3 51.5 AS 22.0 79.0 OC -25.3 133.8

items.title: dashboard
items.text:
Key Type Default What it does bind string 127.0.0.1:8088 The listen address of the dashboard, as host:port. auth_token_env string None. The environment variable with the bearer token. auth_token_file string None. A file with the bearer token. allow_config_edits boolean true Lets the dashboard add and remove nodes, and set the location of a node and of the homelab. Each of these changes writes the config file again. terminal boolean true Lets the dashboard open a shell on a node. hostname string None. The first label of the name of the dashboard at your Traefik, <hostname>.<domain>. Without it, there is no route. access string private Who reaches hostname: private (devices of the VPN only) or public. sso.middleware string None. Necessary with sso. A forward-auth middleware of your Traefik, with its provider, for example authelia@docker. A user who signs in there needs no token. It needs hostname. sso.user_header string Remote-User The header with the name of the user. sso.groups_header string Remote-Groups The header with the groups of the user, with commas between them. sso.groups list [] The groups with full access. With an empty list, each user that is not read-only has full access. sso.read_only_groups list [] The groups that can only look.

The sso object is optional. If neither auth_token_env nor auth_token_file gives a token, HomeGAP creates one in <data_dir>/dashboard-token. See The dashboard.

items.title: speedtest
items.text:
Key Type Default What it does enabled boolean false Enables the speed test endpoints. hostname string speedtest The label of the names <hostname>.<domain> and <hostname>-<node>.<domain>. bind string 0.0.0.0:8089 The listener that the homelab proxy reaches. Never publish it directly. link_ttl duration 2h The lifetime of a test link for a device. phase_seconds integer 8 The duration of each download and upload phase, from 2 to 30. link_budget_gb integer 20 The data that one device link can send and receive in total, in GiB, from 1 to 1000. streams integer 4 The number of parallel TCP streams for a test between the homelab and a node, from 1 to 16. vpn_access boolean false With true, a device of the VPN opens the test page with no link from the dashboard. The front door needs homegap.private_network.

See Speed tests.

items.title: status_page
items.text:
Key Type Default What it does enabled boolean false Enables the public status page. hostname string status The label of the names <hostname>.<domain> and <hostname>-<node>.<domain>. title string Status The heading of the page, 60 characters or fewer.

The listener of speedtest.bind serves the status page. See Status page.

items.title: homelab
items.text: Key Type Default What it does location object None. { latitude, longitude, name }: the location of the homelab, for the maps. The public status page shows only its region. ssh.enabled boolean false Publishes the SSH server of the homelab host as a private service, for devices of the VPN only. See Private services. ssh.hostname string ssh The first label of the name, <hostname>.<domain>. A single lowercase label. ssh.port integer 22 The port of the SSH server of the host. ssh.roles list [] The roles that can reach the host. Admin always can.

items.title: map
items.text: Key Type Default What it does tiles string /usr/share/homegap/map/world.pmtiles The PMTiles archive of the maps. Without it, the maps show markers on a plain background.

items.title: Environment variables
items.text:
Variable Default What it does HOMEGAP_CONFIG /config/config.yml The path of the config file. HOMEGAP_DRY_RUN None. With 1, true or yes, the orchestrator runs in dry run. HOMEGAP_VERSION None. The tag of the default image of the agent on each node (agent.image). The shipped compose file also uses it as the tag of the stack. HOMEGAP_REVISION The commit of the image. The default of agent.revision. DOCKER_SOCKET /var/run/docker.sock The path of the Docker socket. DOCKER_HOST None. The address of the Docker socket proxy, as tcp://host:port. With it, the orchestrator does not use the socket. The shipped compose file sets it. HOMEGAP_MESH_DIR /mesh The directory that the orchestrator and the mesh agent share. HOMEGAP_IDENTITY_DIR /identity The directory of the signed directory of users. The orchestrator writes it and the sign-in reads it. HOMEGAP_SIGN_IN_DIR /sign-in The directory of the sign-in. The orchestrator reads the public key of the sign-in there. HOMEGAP_VPN_DIR /vpn The directory that the sign-in and the mesh agent share for the devices of the VPN. HOMEGAP_DEBUG None. If set, prints stack traces on fatal errors. HOMEGAP_DOCS_DIR /usr/share/homegap/docs The directory where the dashboard finds these docs. HOMEGAP_STACK_FILES /usr/share/homegap/deploy The directory where homegap init finds the files of the homelab stack. HOMEGAP_LEGO lego The path of the Lego binary, which orders the certificate of the nodes.

The default of each of the four shared directories is the mount point of the shipped compose file. If that directory does not exist, HomeGAP uses <data_dir>/mesh, <data_dir>/identity, <data_dir>/sign-in or <data_dir>/vpn.

The orchestrator also reads the variables that your *_env keys name. The sign-in container reads the variable of sign_in.oidc.client_secret_env. See Secrets.

items.title: Secrets
items.text: The config file never holds a secret. This page tells you how to give secrets to HomeGAP, and where HomeGAP keeps the secrets that it creates.

items.title: References to secrets
items.text:
Each secret in the config is a reference:

  • A key that ends in _env names an environment variable.
  • A key that ends in _file names a file that you mount in the container.

The config has these references:

Key Default The secret The container that reads it bunny.api_key_env BUNNY_API_KEY The API key of your Bunny account. orchestrator bunny.api_key_file None. The same key, as a file. orchestrator dashboard.auth_token_env None. The bearer token of the dashboard. orchestrator dashboard.auth_token_file None. The same token, as a file. orchestrator sign_in.oidc.client_secret_env HOMEGAP_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET The client secret of the OpenID Connect provider. homegap-sign-in nodes[].ssh_key_file None. Necessary. The private SSH key of the node. orchestrator

For the Bunny key and the dashboard token, HomeGAP tries these sources in this order:

  1. The environment variable, if it is set and not blank.
  2. The file, if it is set and not blank.
  3. The file /run/secrets/<ENV_NAME>, with the name from the *_env key. This is the convention of Docker secrets.

HomeGAP removes spaces and line breaks at the start and the end of each value.

The Config page on the dashboard lists the Bunny key, the dashboard token and the SSH key of each node. It shows if each one is present or missing. The page never shows the values.

items.title: Environment variables
items.text:
Put the values in .env next to the compose file. homegap init gives the file mode 600. Never commit the file.

BUNNY_API_KEY=...
HOMEGAP_DASHBOARD_TOKEN=...
HOMEGAP_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET=...

The config refers to the variables by their names:

bunny:
  api_key_env: BUNNY_API_KEY
dashboard:
  auth_token_env: HOMEGAP_DASHBOARD_TOKEN
sign_in:
  oidc:
    client_secret_env: HOMEGAP_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET

The shipped compose file gives each variable of .env to the orchestrator. Thus a secret of the orchestrator needs only a line in .env.

items.title: The dashboard token
items.text:
Every /api route of the dashboard needs the bearer token, or a sign-in through dashboard.sso. The orchestrator reads the token one time, at the start.

If the config names no token, or the token that it names is not available, HomeGAP creates one. It keeps the token in dashboard-token in its data directory, with mode 0600. With the shipped stack, this is the file data/orchestrator/dashboard-token. The log of the orchestrator names the file at the start.

items.title: The client secret of the sign-in provider
items.text:
The sign-in runs in its own container, homegap-sign-in. That container does not get the variables of .env. The shipped compose file gives it one variable, HOMEGAP_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET.

With sign_in.oidc in the config, the sign-in container must have the variable that client_secret_env names. If the variable is missing or blank, the container stops with the error sign_in.oidc needs the variable <name> in the sign-in container. The sign-in reads this secret only from the environment variable. It does not read a file or /run/secrets.

To use a different variable name, add the variable to the homegap-sign-in service in compose.override.yml:

services:
  homegap-sign-in:
    environment:
      MY_OIDC_SECRET: ${MY_OIDC_SECRET:-}

After a change of the secret, start the container again:

docker compose up -d homegap-sign-in

See Sign-in.

items.title: The SSH keys of the nodes
items.text:
ssh_key_file of a node is a path in the orchestrator container. With the shipped stack, the path /data/ssh/na1 is the file data/orchestrator/ssh/na1 in the folder of the stack.

The Add node wizard of the dashboard creates an ed25519 key for a new node, or imports a key that you give it. It keeps the key in ssh/ in the data directory, as <id>_ed25519, with mode 0600. The folder has mode 0700. The private key never leaves the orchestrator.

If you add a node by hand, put its private key in data/orchestrator/ssh/. Give the file mode 600 and the owner of the stack folder.

items.title: Docker secrets
items.text:
Docker mounts each secret at /run/secrets/<name>. If the name of the secret is the same as the name in the *_env key, the orchestrator finds it there. Put this in compose.override.yml:

services:
  orchestrator:
    secrets: [HOMEGAP_DASHBOARD_TOKEN]

secrets:
  HOMEGAP_DASHBOARD_TOKEN:
    file: ./secrets/dashboard_token

With dashboard.auth_token_env: HOMEGAP_DASHBOARD_TOKEN and an empty HOMEGAP_DASHBOARD_TOKEN variable, HomeGAP reads /run/secrets/HOMEGAP_DASHBOARD_TOKEN.

Note

The shipped compose file needs BUNNY_API_KEY in .env. Docker Compose refuses to start the stack without it.

items.title: Secrets that HomeGAP creates
items.text:
HomeGAP creates these secrets itself. The folders are the folders of the shipped stack.

Secret Where it is The dashboard token, if the config gives none. data/orchestrator/dashboard-token, with mode 0600. The SSH keys from the Add node wizard. data/orchestrator/ssh/, with mode 0600. The key that signs the directory of users. data/orchestrator/authority/authority.key, with mode 0600. No other container mounts this folder. The key of the sign-in, which signs the sessions of the devices. data/sign-in/issuer.key, with mode 0600. Only the sign-in container writes this folder. The WireGuard keys of the homelab, for the mesh and for the VPN. data/mesh/hg-mesh.key and data/mesh/hg-vpn.key, with mode 0600. The ACME account key, and the certificate of the nodes with its key. data/orchestrator/acme/. The key of the CrowdSec bouncer of each node, with node_stack.crowdsec. The state file data/orchestrator/state.json (mode 0600). On the node, .env and config/traefik/dynamic/homegap-crowdsec.yml, with mode 0600. The mesh key of each node. /etc/wireguard/hg-mesh.key on the node. The node creates it, and the private key never leaves the node. The key of the exit of each node. agent-state/hg-exit.key in the install folder of the node.

HomeGAP does not keep the password of a user or the secret of a machine. It shows each one time, when you create it, and keeps only a hash.

Warning

Keep a backup of data/orchestrator/authority/. The folder holds the users and the key that signs them. Without it, HomeGAP starts with no users and a new key.

For each file, see Files and state. For the full security model, see Security model.

items.title: Build from source
items.text: This page tells you how to build and test HomeGAP, how CI builds the image, and how to contribute.

items.title: Requirements
items.text: You need JDK 21. The build downloads Gradle, Kotlin/Native and Node (for the dashboard) by itself.

items.title: Commands
items.text: Command What it does ./gradlew macosArm64Test Runs the unit tests on an Apple Silicon Mac. The other targets are linuxX64 and linuxArm64. ./gradlew :presentation:jsNodeTest Runs the presenter tests of the dashboard, on Node. ./gradlew linkReleaseExecutableLinuxX64 linkReleaseExecutableLinuxArm64 Builds the two Linux binaries. ./gradlew -Phomegap.skipWeb=true … Skips the dashboard bundle, for fast iteration. ./gradlew :web:jsBrowserDevelopmentServe --continuous Runs the development server of the dashboard. It sends /api to port 8088. tools/build-map.sh tiles Builds map/world.pmtiles for local runs. The image builds its own tiles.

items.title: The image
items.text:
The image build needs the two Linux binaries first:

  1. Build the binaries: 
    ./gradlew linkReleaseExecutableLinuxX64 linkReleaseExecutableLinuxArm64
  2. Build the image: 
    docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t homegap .

The Dockerfile builds the map tiles and these docs (mkdocs.embedded.yml) itself. It also downloads lego, the ACME client, and checks its SHA-256. The image has the files of the homelab stack in /usr/share/homegap/deploy, for homegap init.

One image has every role. The command selects the role: run for the orchestrator, mesh for the mesh agent, sign-in for the sign-in and node-agent for the agent of a node. See Command line.

items.title: CI
items.text:
.github/workflows/build.yml runs on pushes to main, on version tags, on pull requests and on a manual start. It runs the unit tests and the presenter tests. Then it builds one multi-arch image, for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64. On each run that is not a pull request, it publishes the image to GHCR and signs it with cosign. For a version tag, it also adds the archive of the stack files to the GitHub release. The image tags are:

Event Tags A push to main main, sha-<short> A tag vX.Y.Z X.Y.Z, X.Y, X, latest

items.text:

items.title: Contributing
items.text:
Issues and pull requests are welcome. Before you open a pull request, make sure that the unit tests and the presenter tests pass (./gradlew macosArm64Test :presentation:jsNodeTest). For changes to provisioning, routing or DNS, the end-to-end harness must also pass. See End-to-end tests.

For changes to these docs, see Documentation.

items.title: Code style
items.text:
This page gives the rules for the Kotlin code of the orchestrator in src/. The aim is code that a person can read from top to bottom and understand. MeshReconciler.kt is the reference example.

The dashboard code in web/ and presentation/ follows the same rules.

items.title: Behavior
items.text:
A cleanup must not change what the code does.

  • Keep each log message, error message, script, template, wire format and serialized name exactly as it is.
  • Change the structure of a function only if a test or the end-to-end harness covers it. If nothing covers it, make only the changes that cannot change the behavior: a new name, a line break, a constant.
  • Do not change what a test asserts to make a cleanup pass.
  • The tests and the build scripts follow these rules too. A cleanup of a test keeps its name, its calls and its expected values.

items.title: Warnings
items.text:
A file has no warnings from the compiler and no warnings from the inspections of the IDE.

  • Correct the cause of a warning. Do not hide it.
  • Two warnings can have @Suppress, with the reason in a comment or in the KDoc:
    • HttpUrlsUsage, where the code uses plain HTTP on purpose. An example is a request on the mesh, which WireGuard encrypts.
    • unused, on a class or a function that only the dependency graph or a serializer uses.

items.title: Lines and layout
items.text:
• A line has 120 characters or fewer. The text in a raw string (a script, a page, a template) is the exception, because a line break changes the output.
  • When a call or a declaration does not fit on one line, put each argument or parameter on its own line, with a comma after the last one.
  • When a chain of calls does not fit on one line, put each call on its own line.
  • A branch of if, else or when that has more than one line has braces.
  • One statement on each line. Do not use semicolons.
  • Build a long string from parts with names, or from a list that you join. Do not write one long concatenation.

items.title: Functions
items.text:
• A function does one thing. A long function is a short outline that calls functions with clear names, in the order of the work.
  • A function has four parameters or fewer. If it needs more, put the values that belong together in a small class. Then the class can have the function as a member.
  • Use named arguments when a call has more than three arguments, when two arguments have the same type, or when an argument is a literal such as null or true.
  • Do not write a local function that is longer than a few lines. Make it a private function.
  • Return early for the case that ends the work. Do not put the main path in a deep if.

items.title: Names
items.text:
• A name says what the value is: node, result, address. Do not use one letter (n, r, q). The exceptions are it in a short lambda, e for a caught exception, and an index.
  • A number or a string with a meaning is a constant with a name: a timeout, a limit, a marker in the output of a script.
  • Constants are const val in a private companion object, or private const val at the top level.

items.title: Shared code
items.text:
• Do not copy a helper. If two files need the same helper, put it in a shared file and use it in both.
  • To catch the errors of a suspend block, use runCatchingCancellable. It is in homegap.platform for the orchestrator, and in homegap.presentation.core for the dashboard. Do not write try/catch with a check for CancellationException by hand.
  • Use orEmpty(), not ?: "" or ?: emptyList().
  • Use check and require for a condition that throws. Do not write if (...) throw IllegalStateException(...).

items.title: Comments and KDoc
items.text:
• Write few comments. A comment gives the reason for code that does not explain itself. It does not say again what the code does.
  • A public class and a function that is not clear from its name have KDoc. Short KDoc is better than long KDoc.
  • KDoc and comments follow the Writing style guide: the present simple, the active voice, short sentences, no "-ing" forms for actions, no semicolons and no em dashes.
  • Keep a KDoc that is correct and that follows the guide. Change a KDoc only to correct it or to make it follow the guide.
  • Do not keep code in a comment, and do not keep a comment about code that is gone.

items.title: Checks before a commit
items.text:
1. Run the inspections of the IDE on each file that you changed. The result must be empty.
  2. Run the tests: 
    ./gradlew macosArm64Test :presentation:jsNodeTest
  3. For a change in a reconciler, a template or a script, run the end-to-end harness. See End-to-end tests. After the deploy, the first pass must show no changes, and the stack of each node must keep its hash.

items.title: Documentation
items.text: These docs are built with Zensical, from the Material for MkDocs team. Zensical reads mkdocs.yml. This page tells you how to preview and build them, how the versions work and where the dashboard copy comes from.

items.title: Sources
items.text:
• The config is mkdocs.yml.
  • The pages are in docs/.
  • docs/requirements.txt pins the dependencies: zensical 0.1.0, pymdown-extensions 13.0, and the Zensical fork of mike (tag 2.2.0+zensical-0.1.0). The fork is not on PyPI. pip installs it from GitHub, so git must be installed.

The theme is dark (slate), and it uses system fonts. The site loads no fonts from a third party.

items.title: Preview the docs
items.text:
1. Install the dependencies: 
    python3 -m pip install -r docs/requirements.txt
  2. Start the preview server: 
    zensical serve
  3. Open http://localhost:8000.

To build the site as CI does, run a strict build. A broken link or a missing page fails it.

zensical build --strict

The output goes to site/.

items.title: Variables and Jinja
items.text:
Every page goes through Jinja, through Zensical's own version of the markdownextradata plugin. The variable hg_version gives the version that the pages describe. It comes from the VERSION environment variable, with the default dev.

Caution

Literal Jinja delimiters in a page, for example in a Go template for docker inspect, break the build. Put such text in a Jinja raw block.

items.title: Versions
items.text:
.github/workflows/docs.yml builds both configs on each pull request, each push to main and each version tag that changes the docs. It publishes to GitHub Pages (the gh-pages branch) with the Zensical fork of mike, but only when the repository is public:

Event Version A push to main dev A tag vX.Y.Z X.Y, with the alias latest. latest becomes the default.

items.title: The copy in the image
items.text:
The Dockerfile builds mkdocs.embedded.yml into /usr/share/homegap/docs. This config inherits mkdocs.yml, but it has no version selector and no mike. The image build gives it VERSION, and build.yml passes the image version. The image build does not install mike.

The dashboard serves this copy at /docs/, and links it as Documentation at the bottom of the sidebar. To use a different folder, set HOMEGAP_DOCS_DIR. For example, build a local copy and point the orchestrator at it:

zensical build -f mkdocs.embedded.yml
python3 tools/localize-docs-assets.py site-embedded

The output goes to site-embedded/. The script makes the theme load its optional files from the site, not from a CDN. The image build runs the same two commands.

items.title: Writing rules
items.text:
Follow the Writing style guide for every page.

A screenshot that the maintainer must add is an HTML comment on its own line, in this form:

<!-- SCREENSHOT: docs/img/<page>/<nn>-<what>.png | what the image shows -->

The images go in docs/img/.

Do not use Mermaid diagrams. mkdocs.yml does not enable them.

items.title: End-to-end tests
items.text: The e2e/ folder has a self-contained end-to-end harness. This page tells you what the harness contains, how to run it and what it checks.

items.title: The harness
items.text:
e2e/compose.yml has these services, on one private Docker network:

Service What it is node-na1, node-as1 Two fake Ubuntu VPS nodes, each with sshd and its own Docker daemon. node-fr1 A fresh server for the add-node wizard. It is not in the config. homelab-traefik The front door of the simulated homelab, in passthrough mode with a wildcard and a private path. whoami, git, wiki Web services: behind the front door, with passthrough of its own and with terminate. other-door, shop, notes The front door, a public service and a private service of the extra domain other.example.org. echo, rtc, proxy-echo Raw services: one TCP port, a port list with a named service, and a TCP port with PROXY protocol. ssh-jump A private raw TCP service. orchestrator, mesh, mesh-agent, homegap-sign-in, docker-proxy The homelab stack, with the same users and capabilities as deploy/compose.yml. bunny-mock A stand-in for the Bunny API. pebble A local ACME server in place of Let's Encrypt. authelia A real Authelia, as the OpenID Connect provider of the sign-in. viewer A container with curl, in the role of a visitor. client A VPN device: the unmodified olm client of the Pangolin apps. It is in the profile client, so it does not start by default.

e2e/config.e2e.yml is the config of the harness. It enables the sign-in with Authelia, the exits of the nodes and of the homelab, the status page and the speed test.

items.title: Run the harness
items.text:
1. Build the Linux binary for your Docker host. On an amd64 host, use linkReleaseExecutableLinuxX64 instead. 
    ./gradlew linkReleaseExecutableLinuxArm64
  2. Start the harness. It provisions two fake nodes from nothing, over SSH. 
    e2e/run.sh
  3. Run the checks of the data plane: 
    e2e/verify.sh

The dashboard of the harness is at http://127.0.0.1:18088. Its token is in e2e/work/data/dashboard-token.

Two harnesses cannot run at the same time, because they use the same addresses and ports.

items.title: What run.sh does
items.text:
e2e/run.sh does these steps:

  1. It runs e2e/setup.sh, which makes the test material in e2e/work/ if it is missing. This is an SSH key, a test CA with the certificate of the homelab Traefik, and the key and two users of Authelia.
  2. It builds the image homegap:e2e from the local binary, with e2e/image.Dockerfile.
  3. It starts pebble and reads its root certificate. See The certificate of the nodes.
  4. It starts all services with docker compose up -d --build.
  5. It runs e2e/load-images.sh, which loads homegap:e2e into the Docker daemon of each fake node. The agent of a node runs this image, and a node cannot pull a local image from a registry.

items.title: What verify.sh checks
items.text:
e2e/verify.sh does these checks on every node:

  • Passthrough of the root, with the certificate of the origin.
  • The address of the viewer at the homelab, through PROXY protocol (X-Real-Ip).
  • A private-only name returns 403 to the public.
  • A private-only subfolder of the root returns 403 to the public, and the rest of the root returns 200.
  • Passthrough of the wildcard.
  • The sign-in through this node, with the certificate that HomeGAP orders for the nodes.
  • The status page tells a public visitor that it is no VPN device.
  • The shared names of the status page and the speed test, which name this node.
  • The health endpoint on port 80, which Bunny probes.
  • The redirect from HTTP to HTTPS.
  • A dedicated passthrough service, with the certificate of the origin.
  • A dedicated terminate service, with the certificate that HomeGAP orders for the nodes.
  • The certificate on the node has the terminate name and the names of the extra domain. It has no wildcard of the main domain and no passthrough name. The node has no ACME account.
  • Raw TCP on the public port 19000.
  • A port list on TCP (7881 and 3478) and on UDP (3478), and a named service on 17000/udp.
  • Two UDP callers at the same time on port 7882.
  • The dedicated service and the front door of the extra domain.

After the nodes, the script does these checks:

  • A private dashboard returns 403 to the public through each node, and 200 to the private network.
  • homelab.ssh is a private service to the address of the host that the mesh agent found.
  • The zone of the extra domain has the root, the wildcard and shop on each node, and the two CAA records.
  • The main zone has no record of the extra domain, the two CAA records and no challenge record.
  • The dashboard through the sign-in of the homelab Traefik gives 200 to the private network and 403 to the public.

Most checks print the result next to the value to expect. Compare them. The script stops with an error for four checks: the names on the certificate, the private dashboard, the address of the homelab host and the records of the zones.

items.title: The certificate of the nodes
items.text:
The pebble service accepts each challenge without a DNS lookup. Thus the harness checks that HomeGAP writes and removes the challenge records. It does not check that they resolve.

Pebble makes a new root certificate each time its container starts. run.sh reads the root and writes work/certs/trust.pem, which the viewer and the client trust. After a new root, run.sh removes work/data/acme and restarts the orchestrator, so HomeGAP orders the certificate again.

items.title: A VPN device
items.text:
The client service connects to https://signin.test.example.net as a machine. CLIENT_NODE_IP takes the role of DNS: it sends the device to one node. The default is the address of node-as1.

  1. Create a machine. The command prints its id and its secret. 
    docker compose -f e2e/compose.yml exec orchestrator homegap machine add e2e-client
  2. Start the client with the id and the secret. This example sends the device to node-na1. 
    OLM_ID=<id> OLM_SECRET=<secret> CLIENT_NODE_IP=172.30.0.10 docker compose -f e2e/compose.yml --profile client up -d client

The client has its local API on 127.0.0.1:9452 in the container. Use it to read the state of the client and to select an exit.

items.title: Writing style guide
items.text: This page is the brief for everyone who writes HomeGAP documentation, people and agents alike. The rules are a working profile of ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English (STE), adapted for software documentation, plus rules for accuracy and for a natural, human voice.

items.title: Part 0: Role and scope
items.text:
You write and edit the HomeGAP documentation in docs/. You get a brief for each page. The brief lists the facts, the sources in the code, and the order of the page.

  • Use only the facts in the brief, or facts you confirm in the source files that the brief names.
  • Do not add a feature, option, default, number, command, UI label, file path or behavior that the brief or the source does not show.
  • If a fact that you need is not in the brief, and you cannot confirm it in the source, do not guess. Put an HTML comment <!-- FACT-CHECK: what is missing --> at that location and list it in your report.
  • Write only files under docs/. Do not change code, mkdocs.yml or other files, unless the brief tells you to.
  • Use example.net for domains, na1, eu1, as1 for node ids and documentation addresses (203.0.113.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24) for public IP addresses. Never use a real domain, a real person's name or a real location of a user's homelab.

items.title: Part 1: The nine grammatical and structural pillars
Section 1: Words and parts of speech
items.text:
• Rule 1.1: One word, one meaning. Use each word as one part of speech, with one meaning.
    • Use "close" only as a verb ("Close the dialog"). For the adjective, use "near".
    • Use "oil" only as a noun. Write "Apply oil to the bearing", not "Oil the bearing".
  • Rule 1.2: Use verbs for actions, not nouns made from verbs.
    • Not: "Perform an inspection of the seal." / "Execute the alignment."
    • Write: "Inspect the seal." / "Align the component."
  • Rule 1.3: Do not use phrasal verbs.
    • Not: "set up", "put together", "take apart", "carry out", "turn on", "find out".
    • Write: "prepare" or "configure", "assemble", "disassemble", "do", "enable" or "start", "learn" or "find".
    • Exception: a phrasal verb that is a name in a UI or a command (the Add node button, docker compose up) stays as it is.

items.title: Section 2: Noun clusters
items.text:
• Rule 2.1: Not more than three nouns in a row. Break longer clusters with prepositions.
    • Not: "node stack agent container image update".
    • Write: "an update of the agent image in the stack of the node".
    • Exception: a technical name stays as it is (homegap-mesh-agent, "OpenID Connect provider").

items.title: Section 3: Verbs and tenses
items.text:
• Rule 3.1: Use only three verb forms.
    1. The infinitive, for a purpose: "To add a node, ...".
    2. The imperative, for a step: "Open", "Set", "Run".
    3. The present simple, for a description: "The orchestrator reads the labels."
  • Rule 3.2: No compound or future tenses. Use the past participle only as an adjective before a noun ("the saved stack"). Do not write "will", "has been", "will have".
    • Not: "The node will be removed from DNS."
    • Write: "HomeGAP removes the node from DNS."
  • Rule 3.3: Do not use "-ing" forms for actions or states.
    • Not: "While provisioning the node, ..." / "The device is reconnecting."
    • Write: "During provisioning, ..." / "The device connects again."
    • Exception: a technical name or UI text with "-ing" stays as it is (provisioning…, "Waiting for DNS", the waiting for certificate state, ping).

items.title: Section 4: Sentences
items.text:
• Rule 4.1: Word limits.
    • A procedural sentence (a step): 20 words or fewer.
    • A descriptive sentence: 25 words or fewer.
    • Code, labels, paths and URLs count as one word each.
  • Rule 4.2: One idea in each sentence. A sentence can have one dependent clause, if that clause gives a simple condition ("If the mesh link is down, ...").
  • Rule 4.3: No hedging. Do not use should, would, may, might, likely, probably, could, perhaps, usually (unless the code shows a real "usually", give the condition).
    • For a requirement, use must.
    • For a capability, use can.
    • For a recommendation, say it directly: "We recommend ...", or give the reason: "Use sign_in.oidc with a second factor. A node can read a password that a user types."

items.title: Section 5: Procedures
items.text:
• Rule 5.1: One action in each step. Put each action in its own numbered step. A step can have a second sentence that tells the result ("The dashboard shows the node as provisioning….").
  • Rule 5.2: Condition before command. Give the condition, the requirement or the precaution before the action.
    • Not: "Press Run after you test the connection."
    • Write: "Test the connection. Then click Run." or "When the test passes, click Run."

items.title: Section 6: Descriptions
items.text: • Rule 6.1: Not more than six sentences in a paragraph. Do not put descriptive text and numbered steps in the same block. Put the description first, then the procedure.

items.title: Section 7: Safety messages
items.text:
• Rule 7.1: Mark each risk clearly, and isolate it. Start with the condition or the action, then give the risk.
    • Use !!! danger "Warning" when there is a risk of data loss, of lockout from a server, or of exposure of a private service or a secret.
    • Use !!! warning "Caution" when there is a risk of an interruption of service or of a failed operation.
    • Use !!! note for information that is not a risk, and !!! tip for a shortcut.
    • Example: "If you restrict SSH with ssh_allow_from and your public IP address changes, the orchestrator cannot connect to the node."

items.title: Sections 8 and 9: Punctuation and completeness
items.text:
• Rule 8.1: Do not drop words. Keep "the", "a" and "an". Keep verbs. No telegraphic text, also in table cells and list items that are sentences.
  • Rule 8.2: No semicolons. Make two sentences.

items.title: Part 2: Word list (one word, one meaning)
items.text:
Do not use Use begin, commence, initiate start utilize, employ, leverage use terminate, halt, conclude (as general verbs) stop or end perform, execute, carry out the specific verb (do, run, check, install) frequently, periodically the exact interval ("every 60 seconds") or often verify, ascertain, ensure make sure or check permit, allow (as general verbs) let, or say what a person can do set up configure or prepare (and the noun setup) take down stop or remove in order to to via through or with e.g., i.e. "for example", "that is"

Technical names (TN) and technical verbs. Keep words that are names of HomeGAP, Traefik, Bunny, WireGuard, Docker or Linux things, also if STE does not approve them. Examples: "orchestrator", "node", "front door", "passthrough", "terminate" (the TLS mode), "provision", "reconcile", "deploy", "label", "router", "middleware", "allowlist", "mesh", "sign-in", "exit", "failover", "directory", "tunnel", "slot". Write a name the same way every time.

Literal text is outside these rules. Code blocks, inline code, label names, config keys, commands, log lines, error messages and UI labels stay exactly as the source shows them. Quote a UI label in bold (Add node) and a value or key in code (homegap.tls).

items.title: Example 1: No passive voice, no hedging
items.text:
• Input: "It should be ensured that the interface cover is periodically checked by the maintenance crew to prevent any accumulating dust from causing a system malfunction."
  • STE: "The maintenance crew must check the interface cover every week. Dust can cause a system failure."
  • The passive "It should be ensured" and the hedge "should" are gone. The "-ing" form "accumulating" is gone. There are two short sentences, each with one idea.

items.title: Example 2: No noun clusters, no phrasal verbs
items.text:
• Input: "Before carrying out the automated backup system software configuration update, verify that the primary storage drive is completely empty."
  • STE: "Check the primary storage drive. Make sure that it is empty. Then, update the configuration of the software for the automated backup system."
  • The condition comes first. A preposition breaks the noun cluster. The phrasal verb "carrying out" is gone.

items.title: Example 3: HomeGAP text
items.text:
• Input: "Once you've set up the first node, HomeGAP will automatically start routing your traffic through the nearest healthy node, which should give you seamless failover."
  • STE: "When the stack of a node runs, Bunny DNS sends each viewer to the nearest healthy node. If a node fails its health check, Bunny removes it from the answers."

items.title: Part 4: A human voice
items.text:
STE limits the grammar. It does not make the text robotic. Write as an experienced engineer who explains the system to a colleague.

  • Be concrete. Give the real value, the real path and the real result. "The node returns a 503 page about 15 seconds after it loses the homelab" is better than "the system degrades gracefully".
  • Explain why, once. If a rule exists for a reason, give the reason in one sentence. Do not repeat it on the page.
  • Use "you" for the reader and the imperative for steps. Use "HomeGAP" or "the orchestrator" for the software, not "we", except in "We recommend".
  • Vary the sentence length inside the limits. Not every sentence has 20 words.
  • Use prose for explanations and lists for real lists (options, steps, items to check). A page that is only bullets is not acceptable.
  • Bold is for UI labels and for the first use of a defined term. Do not start each list item with a bold phrase. The exception is the feature list on the home page (and in the README), where each item starts with its point in bold.

items.title: Do not use these patterns
items.text:
They show that a text is generated, and they give no information:

  • Marketing words: seamless(ly), robust, powerful, effortless(ly), cutting-edge, game-changer, supercharge, unlock, elevate, streamline, empower, harness, delve, dive into, journey, landscape, realm, tapestry, crucial, vital, pivotal, essential (as filler), comprehensive, simply, just, easily, of course, it's worth noting, it's important to note, note that.
  • Openers and closers: "In this guide, ...", "Let's ...", "Whether you're ... or ...", "Welcome to ...", "In summary", "In conclusion", "That's it!", "Happy hosting!".
  • Rhetorical questions as headings or openers ("Why does this matter?").
  • Groups of three adjectives or three parallel phrases for rhythm only.
  • "Not only ... but also ...", "It's not X, it's Y".
  • Em dashes. Use a period, a comma, a colon or parentheses.
  • Emoji, exclamation marks.
  • A summary at the end of a page that repeats the page.
  • Headings with a colon and a slogan ("Failover: Peace of Mind").

items.title: Part 5: Page format (Zensical)
items.text:
• One # heading at the top: the page title, in sentence case. Then one or two sentences that tell what the page is for.
  • ## for sections, ### for subsections. Do not go deeper than ####.
  • Code blocks have a language: yaml, bash, text, json. Commands that a reader runs are in bash blocks, one command per line, without a $ prompt.
  • Admonitions: see Rule 7.1. Use ??? (a closed block) for long optional detail.
  • Use content tabs (=== "Password" / === "OpenID Connect") when one step is different in two cases.
  • Links between pages are relative paths to the .md file (../reference/security.md#secrets).
  • Tables for reference data (labels, config keys, ports, API routes). Each cell that is a sentence follows the rules above.
  • The hg_version variable (in double braces) gives the version of the docs. Pages go through Jinja: text that has double braces or a brace with a percent sign (for example Go templates) goes in a Jinja raw block.
  • A screenshot that the maintainer must add is an HTML comment on its own line: <!-- SCREENSHOT: docs/img/<page>/<nn>-<what>.png | what the image shows -->.

items.title: Part 6: Process for each page
items.text:
1. Isolate. Divide the brief into descriptions and procedures.
  2. Draft. Write the page in the order of the brief.
  3. Lint. Find and replace the forbidden words, passive voice, "-ing" forms, hedges, semicolons and the patterns in Part 4.
  4. Measure. Make each sentence fit the word limits. Make each paragraph six sentences or fewer.
  5. Check the facts. Compare each statement with the brief or the source. Remove each statement that you cannot connect to a fact.
  6. Report. After you write the files, report the files that you wrote, each FACT-CHECK comment and each fact in the brief that you think is wrong or unclear. Do not explain your edits.

items.title: Getting started
items.text: This page gives the full order of setup. Each step links to the page with the details.

items.title: The order of setup
items.text:
1. Read How HomeGAP works.
  2. Check the Requirements.
  3. Prepare Bunny DNS: a zone and an API key.
  4. Prepare the servers: one VPS for each region.
  5. Install on the homelab: the stack, the config and the secrets. Start in dry run.
  6. Add a node with the wizard on the dashboard, or by hand.
  7. Publish a service and check it.
  8. Configure the sign-in for the VPN.
  9. Add users on the Access page. See Users, machines and devices.
  10. Connect the Pangolin apps.

Steps 8 to 10 are necessary only for the VPN and for private services.

items.title: What the orchestrator does after you start it
items.text:
You do the steps above one time. After that, the orchestrator does this work by itself:

  • It provisions each node: Docker, ufw, Traefik, the maintenance page and the agent of HomeGAP.
  • It keeps the private mesh between the homelab and each node.
  • It orders the certificate of the nodes from Let's Encrypt, for the names that a node terminates.
  • It writes the routes of the Traefik of each node from the labels.
  • It creates the Bunny geo records with their monitors. A new node gets DNS records only after its stack is up.

items.title: Before production
items.text:
Do these checks on the test domain:

  • All nodes are green on the dashboard.
  • Each name resolves to the correct node in each region.
  • Failover works.
  • The change between passthrough and terminate works.

When all checks pass, set domain and bunny.zone to your production domain and its zone. Then move that domain to Bunny DNS.

items.title: Add a node
items.text: The add-node wizard takes a fresh VPS from the initial login of your provider to a provisioned node. This page tells you how to use the wizard, and how to add a node by hand. The stack on the homelab must run first. See Install on the homelab.

items.title: Before you start
items.text:
The wizard writes the node to the config file. Thus dashboard.allow_config_edits must be true (the default), and the config mount of the orchestrator must be writable. Before each write, HomeGAP saves a backup of the file as <config>.bak-<millis>.
