Setup runs on the orchestrator as a background job. You can leave the page while the job runs.

items.title: How setup protects your access
items.text:
Setup logs in one time with the initial credentials, and it does the setup work through that one connection. Only the last check is a second connection: a login with the key of the node. If the server has a login blocker (fail2ban, sshguard or CrowdSec), setup first exempts the address of the orchestrator, as the server sees it. It also removes any current ban on that address.

Setup proves each change before it keeps the change:

  • Before it hardens SSH, setup checks the key login and the passwordless sudo of the new user over a fresh connection.
  • Setup writes the SSH settings to /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/01-homegap.conf, which comes before the drop-in file of cloud-init. It checks the syntax of the file.
  • Setup checks the effective SSH values with sshd -T -C for root, the login user and the management user, from the address of the orchestrator. Thus it finds a Match block that overrides the settings.
  • After the change, a fresh key login must work. If it does not work, setup restores the previous settings.
  • Before a change to the SSH settings or the firewall, setup arms a timer on the node. The timer reverts the change after two minutes. Setup disarms it only after a fresh login works.

If the orchestrator loses the connection to the node during a change, the node reverts the change by itself.

The password is for the setup job only. HomeGAP never writes it to disk or to the config. The password goes to ssh through SSH_ASKPASS, and to sudo on its standard input.

items.title: Open the wizard
items.text:
1. On the dashboard, open Nodes.
  2. Click + Add node. The Add a node wizard opens. It shows "Nothing changes on the server until you run it."

items.title: 1. Server
items.text:
1. In Node id, type the id of the node, for example eu1. Use lowercase letters, digits and dashes. Start with a letter.
  2. In Public IP or host name, type the address of the server.
  3. In SSH port, type the SSH port. The default is 22.
  4. Set the location. Search the known data-center cities (for example "dallas", "london" or "hetzner"), or click a point in Pick on the map.
  5. Optional: correct Region code, Latitude, Longitude or Place name.
  6. Optional: type the Provider.
  7. Click Continue.

When you pick a point on the map, the nearest known city within 50 km gives the point its name.

items.title: 2. Initial login
items.text:
1. In User, type root or another user that can use sudo.
  2. Select Password or Private key.
  3. For Password, type the password.
  4. For Private key, type the path of the key file in Private key on the orchestrator.
  5. Click Test connection.
  6. For a password login to a new server, the page shows "Check the server's fingerprint". Compare the Host key fingerprint with the fingerprint in the console of your provider.
  7. If the fingerprints are the same, click The fingerprint matches. HomeGAP then sends the password and does the test.
  8. Click Continue.

HomeGAP sends a password only to a host key that you confirmed. A server that shows a different key later does not get the password.

You must test the connection before you can continue. The test checks the login and shows this information:

  • The OS, as Connected to <os> <version> (<arch>).
  • Root access: how the user gets root access.
  • Docker: if Docker is installed.
  • Host key: the fingerprint of the host key of the server.
  • Orchestrator seen from: the address of the orchestrator, as the node sees it.

If the host key is different from the last connection, the test reports it. Make sure that the server has a new install. Then click Forget the old host key and retry.

items.title: 3. Access
items.text:
The Management user is "The account HomeGAP manages the node with."

  1. Keep Create a dedicated user selected. The default User name is homegap. This user has passwordless sudo and logs in over SSH with a key only.
  2. Keep Add it to the docker group selected, or clear it. It is selected by default.
  3. Under SSH key, select Generate a new key, Paste a private key or Use a key file on the orchestrator.
  4. Click Generate key or Use this key. The page shows "Key ready" and the fingerprint.
  5. Under SSH hardening, Disable root login is selected by default. Clear it to keep root login. This option needs a management user other than root. If the initial login is not root, and root login is off already or the server keeps it on, setup writes a note in the step and continues.
  6. Disable password login is selected by default. Then SSH accepts keys only, for every user. Clear it to keep password login.
  7. Optional: if the initial login is not root and HomeGAP creates a management user, select Disable SSH login for the initial user. Then that user cannot log in over SSH. The console of your provider still works.
  8. Optional: in New SSH port, type a port for the SSH server of the node. Leave the field empty to keep the port. HomeGAP moves the SSH server after setup, and it keeps the old port open until the new port works. See Node updates and rollback.
  9. Click Continue.

A generated key is an ed25519 key. HomeGAP keeps it in <data dir>/ssh/ on the orchestrator.

HomeGAP runs each script on the node as root, through sudo -n. It then gives the files under the install directory (/opt/homegap by default) to the management user. If the user is in the docker group, docker compose works in that folder without sudo when you log in yourself.

items.title: 4. Firewall
items.text:
1. Keep Let HomeGAP manage the firewall selected. HomeGAP keeps the rules in sync on each provisioning pass.
  2. Under SSH from, select Anywhere or Only these sources.
  3. For Only these sources, check the list in Allowed sources. The wizard fills it with the address from the connection test.
  4. Click Continue.

The page shows the rules under Rules. The firewall of a node opens these ports:

  • SSH on its port (tcp), from anywhere or from the sources in the list.
  • HTTP 80/tcp, HTTPS 443/tcp and 443/udp.
  • The mesh on mesh.port/udp (default 51821).
  • The ports of raw TCP and UDP services, the VPN and the exit of the node. HomeGAP opens them with its own rules, before the rules of ufw.

For the ports, see Prepare the servers.

Warning

This risk applies to Only these sources. If the public IP address of the orchestrator changes to an address outside the list, HomeGAP loses SSH access to the node. This occurs with a residential IP address, a new ISP or a homelab in a new location. Provisioning and health checks for that node then fail until you correct the rule.

Use a stable address range. Or open SSH to anywhere and disable password login.

To recover, log in through the web console of your provider. Run ufw allow <ssh port>/tcp. Then update ssh_allow_from in the config, and click Re-provision for the node. Provisioning replaces the rules of HomeGAP. It does not remove your rule, so delete that rule with ufw delete allow <ssh port>/tcp.

items.title: 5. Review & run
items.text:
1. Examine the summary.
  2. Click Set up and add node. The page shows the progress of each setup step.
  3. Wait until the page shows "Done. Provisioning starts on the next reconcile pass."
  4. Click Go to nodes.

items.title: If setup fails
items.text:
A failed job shows the step with the failure and the reason. Correct the cause, then click Retry.

You can run setup again safely. The completed steps are idempotent. If an earlier run already disabled password login, setup continues with the key of the node.

items.title: After the wizard
items.text:
Provisioning runs in the background. The first install takes a few minutes for Docker, the firewall, the mesh and the stack of the node. During this time, the node shows the current phase on the Nodes page, for example preparing the host (1 of 3).

A new node gets its DNS records only after its stack is up. The node serves viewers when the certificate order with its management name (node-<id>.<domain>) is complete. To see the order, open the Certificates page.

If the first provisioning fails, HomeGAP tries again after five minutes. To try again at once, click Re-provision.

When the node is healthy, continue with Publish a service.

items.title: Add a node by hand
items.text: You can also prepare the server yourself and add the node to nodes[] in the config. See the "By hand" tab in Prepare the servers.

items.title: Prepare Bunny DNS
items.text: HomeGAP uses Bunny DNS to send each viewer to the nearest healthy node. This page tells you how to prepare the DNS zone and the API key.

items.title: What HomeGAP needs
items.text:
HomeGAP needs two things from Bunny:

  • A DNS zone that is equal to domain or a parent of it. The config key is bunny.zone. Validation fails if the zone is not equal to domain or a parent of it.
  • The API key of your Bunny account. The orchestrator reads it from an environment variable (default name BUNNY_API_KEY, config key bunny.api_key_env) or from a file (bunny.api_key_file).

HomeGAP sends the key in the AccessKey header to https://api.bunny.net. It finds the zone by its name and creates all the records itself. You do not create records.

items.title: Prepare the zone and the key
items.text:
1. Choose a test domain. Use a spare domain, or a subdomain of your real domain, for example gap.example.net.
  2. Sign in to Bunny (bunny.net). Open the DNS section at https://dash.bunny.net/dns/zones.
  3. Add a DNS zone for the domain or the subdomain.
  4. Point the domain at the nameservers of Bunny. Do the step that matches your domain:
    • For a whole domain, go to your registrar. Replace the nameservers with the nameservers that Bunny shows for the zone.
    • For a subdomain, go to the current DNS provider of the parent zone. Add NS records for the subdomain there.
  5. Wait until Bunny shows the zone as active. To check the delegation, run this command: 
    dig NS gap.example.net +short
    The command shows the nameservers of Bunny.
  6. Copy the API key of your account from the Bunny account settings at https://dash.bunny.net/account/api-key.
  7. Keep the key for the install. You put it in .env as BUNNY_API_KEY. See Install on the homelab.

items.title: Records at the names that HomeGAP manages
items.text:
Warning

On each DNS sync that is not a dry run and not paused, HomeGAP deletes records that collide with its managed record sets. This occurs at each name that HomeGAP manages: the root, *.<domain>, the dedicated hostnames, the management names of the nodes and the other managed names.

  • HomeGAP deletes an A or AAAA record that it did not create, if it has the same name and type as a managed record.
  • With acme.caa: true (the default), HomeGAP deletes a CAA record at <domain> that it did not create.
  • HomeGAP deletes any CNAME record at a managed name.
  • HomeGAP adopts an unmanaged record that has exactly the desired value.

Before you disable dry run, open the Config page on the dashboard. Find the delete rows in the diff, and write down the records that you want to keep.

HomeGAP never touches records at other names. It marks its own records with the comment managed-by:homegap <purpose> node=<id>.

items.title: What HomeGAP creates
items.text:
Name Record When <domain> A geo record set (the front door). When a front door exists. *.<domain> A geo record set (the front door). When the front door has homegap.wildcard: "true". A public dedicated hostname A geo record set. For each public service with its own hostname. node-<id>.<domain> A plain record (the management name of the node). For each node. The name of sign_in.url A geo record set (the sign-in). With sign_in.url. speedtest.<domain> A geo record set for the speed test. With the speed test, and only if there is no wildcard. speedtest-<node>.<domain> A record for each node. With the speed test. status.<domain> A geo record set. With the status page. status-<node>.<domain> A record for each node. With the status page. <domain> Two CAA records. With acme.caa: true (the default). _acme-challenge.<name> A TXT record. During a certificate order. HomeGAP removes it after the order.

HomeGAP creates A records, and AAAA records for nodes with public_ipv6. The TTL of these records comes from bunny.ttl (default 60). The monitor comes from bunny.monitor (default http). Only geo records get a monitor.

For the routing and the monitors, see DNS routing and health checks.

items.title: Publish a service
items.text: This page tells you how to send the first real traffic through HomeGAP, and how to check the result. You must have one node or more. See Add a node.

items.title: Publish through the front door
items.text:
The front door claims the root domain and *.<domain>. Thus HomeGAP publishes the root and each name one label under the domain that your homelab Traefik serves, and you add no more labels.

To publish a service, add a normal Traefik router at home, for example with the rule Host(`whoami.example.net`).

A service that needs its own path gets its own homegap.* labels. This applies to a dedicated hostname, a raw TCP or UDP service and a private service. See the Label reference. A Docker event starts a pass after a short debounce, so the change does not wait for the next resync.

items.title: Check the service
items.text:
Run these commands from any network:

dig +short example.net
dig +short whoami.example.net
curl -sv https://whoami.example.net/ 2>&1 | grep -E 'subject:|HTTP/'
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://203.0.113.10/

The results are as follows:

  • The two dig commands return node addresses. The wildcard record covers whoami.
  • The curl command to https:// shows the certificate of your homelab. In passthrough mode, the homelab Traefik ends TLS.
  • The curl command to http://<node ip>/ sends the same request as the Bunny monitor. The node sends the request over the mesh to the health check path of the front door (homegap.healthcheck). The command prints the status code of that path.

On the dashboard, the Overview and Services pages show the health in each region. The DNS page shows the records and the state of their monitors.

Note

One node gives no failover. With a single record for each name, Bunny continues to answer with that node when it is down. For failover, you need a second node.

items.title: Label errors
items.text:
The dashboard and the log show label errors for each container. An error in the labels of one container never stops the other services. These are examples of errors:

  • An unknown protocol.
  • The maintenance page (homegap.maintenance_page) without homegap.tls: terminate.
  • A reserved public port.
  • A hostname that two services claim.

An unknown homegap.* label gives a warning, and HomeGAP ignores it.

items.title: Next steps
items.text: For a service that only your own devices can reach, see Private services. For the sign-in of those devices, see Sign-in.

items.title: How HomeGAP works
items.text: This page gives the model of the system: the parts, the path of a request, the VPN, the reconcile loop and failover. Later pages give the details.

items.title: The parts
items.text:
Part What runs there Homelab Docker, the homelab Traefik (the front door), your services and the HomeGAP stack. Nodes Traefik (ports 80 and 443), the maintenance page (homegap-maintenance) and the agent of HomeGAP (homegap-agent). With node_stack.crowdsec, also CrowdSec. Bunny DNS The DNS zone for your domain, with geo routing and health monitors.

The HomeGAP stack on the homelab has these containers:

Container Job orchestrator The control plane (homegap run). It reads the labels and the config, and it writes the nodes, the mesh and the DNS records. homegap-mesh A small container that holds the network namespace of the mesh. homegap-mesh-agent Keeps the WireGuard interface, the forwards to your containers and the home end of the VPN in that namespace. homegap-sign-in The public sign-in for the apps of the VPN. docker-proxy A read-only filter on the Docker socket. The orchestrator reads containers and events through it.

The mesh is a private WireGuard network (hg-mesh) between the homelab and each node. It is always on. Every route from a node to the homelab goes over it. The homelab has no inbound ports: it dials out to each node, so it works behind NAT. For the addresses and the keys, see The mesh.

items.title: The path of a request
items.text:
This is the default path: the front door in passthrough mode.

  1. A viewer resolves a name. Bunny DNS answers with the nearest healthy node.
  2. The viewer connects to that node on port 443.
  3. The Traefik of the node reads the TLS server name. It matches the root domain or any single label under the domain.
  4. Traefik sends the stream, still encrypted, to the mesh address of the homelab.
  5. The mesh namespace of the homelab forwards the stream to the homelab Traefik.
  6. The homelab Traefik ends TLS and routes the request to the service.

The node never sees plaintext. Authelia and the other parts of your homelab continue to work without changes.

There are two other paths. With homegap.tls: terminate, the node ends TLS for the name. HomeGAP orders the certificate of the node from Let's Encrypt with the DNS challenge, only for the names that a node terminates. For a raw TCP or UDP port, the kernel of the node forwards the packets over the mesh. See Traffic paths and Raw ports.

The orchestrator never carries traffic. It talks to the nodes over SSH, to the mesh agent through a shared folder, and to Bunny through the Bunny API.

items.title: Sign-in and VPN
items.text:
HomeGAP has its own sign-in for the Pangolin apps and the olm client. The address of the sign-in is sign_in.url, and each node serves it. A user signs in with a HomeGAP password or through an OpenID Connect provider.

A device of the VPN connects to a node, and the node forwards it to the homelab. Private services get names that only the devices of the VPN resolve and reach. The roles of the user decide which private services a device can reach. HomeGAP denies everything else.

A device can also select an exit. Then all its traffic leaves for the internet from a node or from the homelab. See Sign-in and VPN.

items.title: Reconciliation
items.text:
The orchestrator is a reconciler. It moves the actual state toward the desired state. The desired state is the Docker labels and the config file, and nothing else.

The work has independent domains. A failure in one domain does not stop the others.

Domain What it does Discovery Reads the homegap.* labels from Docker, through the docker-proxy container. Nodes Uses SSH to change a bare Ubuntu VPS into a node: Docker, ufw, the stack and a final check. A drift check at an interval (default 5m) finds changes from outside HomeGAP. Mesh Gives each node a permanent slot and a mesh address. Keeps the WireGuard peers of the homelab and of each node. Routes Writes the routes of the Traefik of each node, and the forwards of raw ports. Traefik loads the routes without a restart. DNS Keeps the Bunny geo record sets for the root, the wildcard and each dedicated hostname. Also keeps a plain record for the management name of each node, node-<id>.<domain>.

A pass is one run of the reconcile loop. Passes start in three ways:

  • On Docker events, after a debounce (default 2s).
  • At an interval, as a full resync (default every 60s).
  • On demand, with Resync on the dashboard.

items.title: Health and failover
items.text:
Each geo record has a Bunny monitor (bunny.monitor, default http). Bunny sends a request to http://<node-ip>/. The node sends this request over the mesh to the health check path of the front door (homegap.healthcheck). Thus a node is healthy only when the node is up, its mesh link is up and the origin answers.

Bunny removes the offline members from a record set. Viewers then resolve to the next-nearest node. The records have a TTL of 60 seconds (bunny.ttl), so a failover also waits for the caches of the resolvers.

When the homelab is down, a node serves the maintenance page for the names for which the node ends TLS. The node checks the homelab every 2 seconds. After three failed checks in a row, it answers with the page and HTTP status 503. For a passthrough name, the node closes the connection at once, because it holds no certificate for the name.

When the homelab is down, a node also signs devices in for the exits only. The exits through a node continue to work. The private services of the homelab do not.

For the monitors and the routing options, see DNS routing and health checks. For each failure and its effect, see Failure modes.

items.title: Install on the homelab
items.text: This page tells you how to put the HomeGAP stack in a folder on the homelab and start it. You do not edit the compose file of the stack: your settings go in files of your own. The first start is a dry run, so that you can examine the changes before HomeGAP makes them.

items.title: The image
items.text: The image is ghcr.io/drewcarlson/homegap, for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64. The same image runs the orchestrator (homegap run), the mesh agent (homegap mesh), the sign-in (homegap sign-in) and the agent of each node. It also holds the files of the stack.

items.title: Get the files
items.text: Make an empty folder for the stack on the homelab. Then get the files in one of these two ways.

items.title: With the image
items.text:
Run homegap init in the folder:

docker run --rm -it -v "$PWD:/work" ghcr.io/drewcarlson/homegap init

The command writes the files of The folder, and it makes the data folders. It gives them to the owner of the folder. If the owner is not user 1000 and group 1000, the command adds HOMEGAP_UID and HOMEGAP_GID to .env. The config file config/config.yml starts with the settings that most homelabs need, and with dry run on.

items.title: With the release archive
items.text:
Each release has the archive homegap-<version>.tar.gz, with the same files.

  1. Download the archive of the newest release.
  2. Extract the archive. The files are in the folder homegap.
  3. Go to the folder homegap.
  4. Copy .env.example to .env.
  5. Make the data folders: 
    mkdir -p data/orchestrator data/mesh data/identity data/sign-in data/vpn
  6. Make the folder of the orchestrator private: 
    chmod 700 data/orchestrator
  7. If id -u or id -g does not print 1000, set HOMEGAP_UID and HOMEGAP_GID in .env to your values.

The orchestrator runs as the owner of the folder, not as root. Docker makes a missing folder as root, so the data folders must exist before the first start.

items.title: The folder
items.text:
Configuration filesHomeGAP files

These are the files that you work with.

Path Content .env The secrets and the variables of the stack. Use mode 600, and never commit this file. config/config.yml The config file, with the settings that most homelabs need. compose.override.yml Your changes to the stack. This file is optional, and you make it yourself. compose.yml The compose file of the stack. Do not edit it. upgrade.sh The upgrade script. See Upgrade the homelab. .env.example, compose.override.example.yml, config/config.example.yml Examples of the variables, the usual changes to the stack and the common config keys.

HomeGAP writes these folders. You do not edit them.

Path Content data/orchestrator/ The state of the orchestrator, the SSH keys of the nodes, the key that signs the directory of users, and the dashboard token. data/mesh/ The description of the mesh for the mesh agent, and the mesh key of the homelab. data/identity/ The signed directory of users, machines and private services. data/sign-in/ The key and the devices of the sign-in. data/vpn/ The devices that are connected. .homegap/ A copy of each file of the stack, as HomeGAP wrote it. With the copies, HomeGAP finds the files that you changed.

An upgrade replaces compose.yml, upgrade.sh and the example files with the files of the new version. It never changes .env, config/config.yml or compose.override.yml. You can run homegap init again at any time, for example to get a file back. See Command line.

Include data/ and config/ in the backup of the homelab. The folder data/ holds every credential, so keep the backup private.

For each variable of .env, the image tags, the content of data/ and the services of the stack, see Homelab stack.

items.title: Install
items.text:
1. Get the files. See Get the files.
  2. Open config/config.yml in an editor.
  3. In config/config.yml, set domain, bunny.zone and acme.email.
  4. Read Certificates. HomeGAP publishes CAA records for your domain, and they also apply to the Traefik of your homelab.
  5. To add the nodes by hand, replace nodes: [] with your nodes. To use the wizard of the dashboard, keep nodes: []. The wizard writes each node to the config file.
  6. Keep reconcile.dry_run: true for the first start.
  7. Set the secrets in .env: 
    BUNNY_API_KEY=...
HOMEGAP_DASHBOARD_TOKEN=...
    For HOMEGAP_DASHBOARD_TOKEN, use a long random string.
  8. If you set no dashboard token, read the token that HomeGAP creates after the first start. It is in the file data/orchestrator/dashboard-token.
  9. Make sure that only you can read the file .env: 
    chmod 600 .env
  10. Make sure that the Docker network of your Traefik exists. If its name is not traefik, set TRAEFIK_NETWORK in .env.
  11. Add the front door labels to your homelab Traefik container: 
    labels:
  homegap.expose: "example.net"
  homegap.wildcard: "true"
  homegap.protocol: "https"
  homegap.tls: "passthrough"
    If the HTTPS entrypoint of Traefik does not listen on 443 inside its container, also add homegap.port: "<that port>".
  12. Add the HTTP provider of HomeGAP to the static configuration of your homelab Traefik: 
    providers:
  http:
    endpoint: http://orchestrator:8088/api/traefik/homelab
    pollInterval: 30s
  13. Recreate the Traefik container, so that it gets the labels and the provider.
  14. Start the services: 
    docker compose up -d
  15. Look at the log of the orchestrator: 
    docker compose logs -f orchestrator
  16. Check the config: 
    docker compose exec orchestrator homegap validate
    The command prints OK: N node(s), domain ..., zone ..., or the list of errors.

The config loader is strict. A key that HomeGAP does not know stops the start.

items.title: The HTTP provider
items.text:
HomeGAP uses the HTTP provider to give your Traefik its own routes. One route sends the names of the speed test and the status page to the orchestrator, when you enable them. With a second route, Traefik answers 421 for the names that only the nodes serve. See Speed tests and Traffic paths.

Keep your other providers. Traefik can use the file provider and the HTTP provider at the same time. The address is the dashboard of the orchestrator, on the traefik network. The dashboard must listen on that network: dashboard.bind: 0.0.0.0:8088, as in the config that homegap init writes. Traefik does not need the dashboard token for this address.

items.title: Open the dashboard
items.text:
Warning

Never expose the dashboard publicly. The dashboard has control of every node.

The stack publishes the dashboard only on the loopback address of the homelab, at port 8088. For a first look, use an SSH tunnel from your workstation.

  1. On your workstation, open the SSH tunnel: 
    ssh -L 8088:127.0.0.1:8088 <homelab>
  2. Open http://localhost:8088 in your browser. The dashboard asks for the token: your HOMEGAP_DASHBOARD_TOKEN, or the token that HomeGAP created.

For the long term, give the dashboard a name at your Traefik, for the devices of the VPN only. See The dashboard.

items.title: Disable dry run
items.text:
In dry run, the orchestrator does full discovery and writes the desired state to the log. It makes no SSH, API or DNS writes.

  1. Open the Config page on the dashboard.
  2. Examine the diff between the desired state and the actual state.
  3. Make sure that each secret in the config shows as present. The page never shows the values.
  4. Set reconcile.dry_run: false in config/config.yml. The orchestrator reads the file again on each pass, so you do not restart it.

If you use HOMEGAP_DRY_RUN instead, remove it from .env. Then run docker compose up -d to recreate the container.

items.title: Add the first node
items.text:
The stack runs, but no node carries traffic until you add one.

  1. Create a server. See Prepare the servers.
  2. Add the node with the wizard of the dashboard. See Add a node.
  3. Wait until the Nodes page shows the node as healthy.
  4. Check the front door through the node. See Publish a service.

After the stack of the node is up, HomeGAP creates the DNS records of the node. Your domain then resolves to the node, and the node sends each request over the mesh to your homelab Traefik.

items.title: Sign-in and VPN
items.text: Without sign_in.url, there is no sign-in and no VPN. To let the Pangolin apps connect, set sign_in.url and add users. See Sign-in.

items.title: Dry run reference
items.text:
Each of these starts the orchestrator in dry run:

  • The environment variable HOMEGAP_DRY_RUN with the value true, 1 or yes.
  • The option --dry-run of homegap run.
  • The config key reconcile.dry_run: true.

To see what a set of labels produces without Docker, use homegap plan:

homegap plan --labels labels.json

The file labels.json is a JSON map of container names to labels.

If you make an edit to the config that is not valid, the orchestrator writes the error to the log. The last good config stays in effect.

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
This page lists what you must have before you install HomeGAP.

Component Requirement Homelab Linux with WireGuard in the kernel, Docker with Compose, and a Traefik instance in front of your services. Regional nodes A VPS with Ubuntu 22.04, 24.04, 26.04 or 26.10 (x86_64 or aarch64), a public IPv4 address (IPv6 is optional) and SSH access. DNS A Bunny DNS zone and a Bunny API key.

One node is sufficient to start. For failover, you need two or more nodes.

items.title: The homelab
items.text:
The compose file of the stack expects the Docker network of your Traefik as an external network with the name traefik. If your network has a different name, set TRAEFIK_NETWORK in .env.

The mesh agent makes the WireGuard interface hg-mesh in a network namespace of its own. Thus the kernel of the homelab host must have WireGuard. WireGuard is part of Linux 5.6 and later.

items.title: SSH access to the nodes
items.text:
HomeGAP accepts two types of SSH access:

  • Root, or a user with sudo, with a password or a key. The add-node wizard prepares the rest. See Add a node.
  • A user with passwordless sudo and a key that you configure yourself. See Prepare the servers.

items.title: Network access
items.text:
The orchestrator needs outbound access to these destinations:

  • The nodes, over SSH.
  • The Bunny API at api.bunny.net. The config key bunny.api_url sets the URL (default https://api.bunny.net).
  • The ACME server of Let's Encrypt, for the certificate of the nodes. The config key acme.directory sets the URL.
  • The nameservers of the zone, for DNS queries.

The mesh agent of the homelab needs outbound UDP access to the mesh port of each node (mesh.port, default 51821).

The Docker daemon of the homelab and the nodes need access to the container registries.

The homelab needs no inbound access. For the ports that a node opens, see Prepare the servers.

items.title: Prepare the servers
items.text: This page tells you what to create at your VPS provider. It also gives the two ways to give HomeGAP access to the servers.

items.title: Create the servers
items.text:
Create one VPS for each region. You can use any provider. Each server must have:

  • Ubuntu 22.04, 24.04, 26.04 or 26.10.
  • An x86_64 or aarch64 CPU.
  • A public IPv4 address. IPv6 is optional.

Write down the public IP address, the SSH port and the initial login that the provider gives you. The initial login is a root password or a key.

items.title: The firewall on the node
items.text:
By default, HomeGAP manages ufw on each node (nodes[].firewall, default true). The firewall denies incoming connections and opens only these ports:

  • SSH, from anywhere or only from the sources in ssh_allow_from.
  • 80/tcp, 443/tcp and 443/udp, for Traefik.
  • mesh.port/udp (default 51821), for the mesh.

HomeGAP opens three more groups of ports with its own rules, which come before the rules of ufw:

  • The public ports of raw TCP and UDP services, as their labels set them.
  • vpn.port/udp (default 51830), for the devices of the VPN.
  • vpn.exit_port/udp (default 51840), on a node that is an exit.

A firewall at the provider level (for example a security group) is outside the control of HomeGAP. It must also open the same ports. For the full list, see Ports.

HomeGAP installs Docker on the node if Docker is not there (install_docker, default true).

items.title: Give HomeGAP access
items.text:
With the wizard (recommended)By hand

Keep the initial root login from your provider, with its password or its key. You do not prepare anything else on the server.

When the orchestrator runs, continue at Add a node. The wizard uses the initial login to create the management user and the SSH key.

Create a user with passwordless sudo and a dedicated SSH key for each node. Then add the node to nodes[] in the config.

First get the files of the stack. See Install on the homelab. Then run these commands on the homelab, in the folder of the stack. Replace the user, the address and the node id with your values.

  1. Create the folder for the keys: 
    mkdir -p data/orchestrator/ssh
  2. Create a key for the node: 
    ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N '' -C homegap-na1 -f data/orchestrator/ssh/na1
  3. Make the private key readable only by you: 
    chmod 600 data/orchestrator/ssh/na1
  4. Copy the public key to the server: 
    ssh-copy-id -i data/orchestrator/ssh/na1.pub deploy@203.0.113.10
  5. Give the user passwordless sudo: 
    ssh -t -i data/orchestrator/ssh/na1 deploy@203.0.113.10 'echo "deploy ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL" | sudo tee /etc/sudoers.d/homegap >/dev/null && sudo chmod 440 /etc/sudoers.d/homegap'
  6. Test the login and sudo: 
    ssh -i data/orchestrator/ssh/na1 -o BatchMode=yes deploy@203.0.113.10 'sudo -n true && echo ok'
    The command must print ok without a prompt.
  7. Add the node to nodes[] in config/config.yml: 
    nodes:
  - id: na1
    region: NA
    host: 203.0.113.10
    ssh_user: deploy
    ssh_key_file: /data/ssh/na1
    location: { latitude: 40.71, longitude: -74.01, name: "New York" }

The ssh_key_file path is the path inside the orchestrator container. The compose file mounts data/orchestrator at /data. The add-node wizard keeps the keys that it makes in the same folder.

The command homegap init makes the folder data/orchestrator with you as its owner. The orchestrator runs as the same user, so it can read the keys.

These rules apply to the entry:

  • The node id must match ^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,30}$. It has lowercase letters, digits and dashes, and it starts with a letter.
  • If host is not an IPv4 address, set public_ipv4.
  • With bunny.routing: geolocation (the default), each node needs a location or a known region code. The codes are NA, SA, EU, AF, ME, AS and OC.

For all the node keys, see the Configuration reference.

items.title: The dashboard
items.text:
The orchestrator serves a dashboard on dashboard.bind. This page tells you how to reach it safely and what each page shows.

Warning

A person with the dashboard token can control every node. Keep the dashboard private: serve it to VPN devices only, or reach it through an SSH tunnel. Make it public only if you accept that the token is then the only protection.

items.title: Serve the dashboard through your Traefik
items.text:
HomeGAP can give the dashboard a name at the Traefik of your homelab, for example orc.example.net. Your Traefik then serves it over HTTPS with its own certificate. You set the name in the config file. The compose file needs no labels.

dashboard:
  bind: 0.0.0.0:8088
  hostname: orc
  access: private
Key Default What it does dashboard.hostname None. The first label of the name, <hostname>.<domain>. Without it, Traefik gets no route for the dashboard. dashboard.access private private serves the name to VPN devices only. public serves it to everybody.

The route comes through the HTTP provider that you added to Traefik during the installation. See Install on the homelab. The name of the route is homegap-dashboard. dashboard.bind must be 0.0.0.0:8088, so that Traefik can reach the dashboard.

items.title: Private access
items.text:
With access: private, only a device on the VPN reaches the name. This mode uses the private path of the front door, so the front door must have the label homegap.private_network. See Client addresses and private-only services.

HomeGAP then does two things:

  • It makes the name a private name of the front door. VPN devices resolve it to the address of the front door on the private network.
  • It adds an allowlist to the route. The allowlist admits only the range of the private network. A request that comes through a node from the internet gets a 403.

A computer on your home network also gets a 403, because it does not come from the private network. Connect that computer to the VPN, or use the address of dashboard.bind.

If the front door has no homegap.private_network, the dashboard gets no route. The Services page then shows the label error "dashboard.access is private, but the front door has no homegap.private_network".

items.title: Public access
items.text:
With access: public, the name answers on the internet, as each other name of the front door does.

Warning

A public dashboard has only the token between the internet and your nodes. A person who gets the token can change the config, remove nodes and open a shell on a node. Use a long token that nothing else uses, and set dashboard.terminal: false if you do not need the terminal.

HomeGAP limits wrong tokens. An address that sends more than 20 wrong tokens in one minute gets no access for the remainder of that minute.

items.title: Sign in with a service such as Authelia
items.text:
If the Traefik of your homelab has a forward-auth middleware, for example of Authelia, HomeGAP can use it for the dashboard. A user who signs in there needs no dashboard token. The dashboard must have a name at your Traefik (dashboard.hostname).

This sign-in is for the dashboard only. The sign-in of the Pangolin apps is a different part. See Sign-in.

dashboard:
  bind: 0.0.0.0:8088
  hostname: orc
  access: private
  sso:
    middleware: authelia@docker
    groups: [admins]
    read_only_groups: [family]
Key Default What it does dashboard.sso.middleware None. The middleware as Traefik names it, with its provider, for example authelia@docker or authelia@file. dashboard.sso.groups Empty. The groups with full access. dashboard.sso.read_only_groups Empty. The groups that can only look. A request from such a user that changes something gets a 403. dashboard.sso.user_header Remote-User The header with the name of the user. dashboard.sso.groups_header Remote-Groups The header with the groups of the user, with commas between them.

The middleware must add the two headers to the request. In Traefik, these are the authResponseHeaders of the forward-auth middleware.

The groups give the role of a user:

  • A user in a group of groups has full access.
  • A user in a group of read_only_groups can only look.
  • With no groups in the config, each other user has full access.
  • With groups in the config, a user in none of the lists gets no access. The dashboard then asks for the token.

items.title: How it works
items.text:
HomeGAP adds two middlewares to the route homegap-dashboard, after the allowlist of private access. The first one removes the sign-in headers from the request of the client, so a client cannot write them. The second one is your middleware. Traefik asks the sign-in service for each request. The orchestrator accepts the headers only from the front door container, and only for the name of the dashboard.

Warning

Do not make a route of your own to the dashboard. On such a route, a client can write the sign-in headers and get full access.

When the session at the sign-in service ends, the dashboard shows the token dialog. Load the page again to sign in.

items.title: When the sign-in service does not work
items.text:
The sign-in is only on the route of your Traefik. The stack publishes the address of dashboard.bind on the loopback address of the homelab, and that address never uses the sign-in. If the sign-in service or Traefik fails, open that address through an SSH tunnel and use the dashboard token. See Install on the homelab.

Three cases are useful to know:

  • The sign-in service is down. The name of the dashboard gives an error. Use the SSH tunnel.
  • You publish the sign-in service through HomeGAP and you pause its service. Sessions that exist continue, because Traefik asks the sign-in service on the Docker network.
  • The dashboard has private access. The browser of a VPN device must also reach the name of the sign-in service, or the sign-in page does not open.

The token always gives full access. Each script and each API client continues to use it.

items.title: The token and the live data
items.text:
A bearer token protects the /api routes. Two routes have their own check. The terminal WebSocket uses a one-time ticket, which a request with the token gets. The Traefik of the homelab can read /api/traefik/homelab from the front door container without the token.

Set the token with dashboard.auth_token_env or dashboard.auth_token_file. If the config names no token, or the token is not available, HomeGAP creates one. It keeps that token in the file dashboard-token in its data directory, with mode 0600. To read the token, run this command:

docker compose exec orchestrator cat /data/dashboard-token

The dashboard asks for the token in a sign-in dialog and keeps it in the browser. To remove the token from the browser, click Sign out at the bottom of the menu. Do this on a computer that other people use.

The dashboard updates live through one server-sent event stream (/api/events). After the first snapshot, the stream sends only the parts that change. When the browser tab is hidden for 30 seconds, the dashboard closes the stream. It opens the stream again when you return to the tab.

The orchestrator writes to the stream at least every 25 seconds. If the dashboard gets nothing for 60 seconds, it opens a new stream. The orchestrator keeps 32 streams open at most. A dashboard above that number gets an error until a different one closes.

If the dashboard cannot reach the orchestrator for more than 5 seconds, the dialog Connection lost opens. It shows the error and the time to the next try, and it has Reconnect now. It closes by itself when the orchestrator answers again. Until then, the page shows the last data from the orchestrator.

items.title: The layout
items.text:
The menu has two groups. Operate has Overview, Nodes, Services, Access and Speed test. Plumbing has DNS, Activity, Diagnostics and Config. A number next to a page is the count of items that need attention there. On a tablet the menu is a rail of icons. On a phone it is one row of pages under the header.

The box at the bottom of the menu shows the last pass, and two controls:

  • Resync queues a pass now.
  • Pause all stops all changes everywhere. The dashboard asks you to confirm first. HomeGAP then only observes, and every page shows a banner with Resume.

During a pause, the box has Resume all and Run one pass. Run one pass applies the changes that wait, and HomeGAP stays paused. An action that changes something during a pause asks you first: Apply just this or Resume everything.

Each page starts with a headline that states the answer, for example "5 of 6 nodes serve.". A node with a warning still serves, and the headline gives the count of such nodes. Under the headline, a status line shows the most important message. When there are more, +N more opens the other messages.

Select a node, a service or another item to open it in the Inspector. On a desktop the Inspector is a drawer on the right that does not block the page. On a tablet it is a drawer over the page, and on a phone it is a sheet at the bottom. The Inspector holds the actions for the item. When an item has more than three actions, one is a button and the others are in More.

Press ⌘K, Ctrl+K or / to search everything. The search finds nodes, services, DNS records, pages, actions such as Resync now, log entries and config keys. Type > to see only the actions. The search shows the names of config keys and secrets, never their values.

Actions that are risky ask first. An action that you cannot undo, such as Decommission, also asks you to type the name. After you remove a node, a message with Undo shows for 30 seconds. Undo adds the node again with its config.

items.title: Overview
items.text:
The Overview page shows the whole system:

  • The gauges: Nodes healthy, Mesh links, Services healthy and DNS healthy.
  • Needs attention: what is wrong now, with the failures first. Select an item to inspect it.
  • Network: Traffic path or Map. The traffic path shows the homelab, then one row for each node with its mesh link and its names. The page remembers your choice. See Maps and locations.
  • Nodes, last hour: one card for each node, with the chart Requests served.
  • Services by node: the response time of each service through each node, in milliseconds.
  • System and recent changes.

items.title: Nodes
items.text:
The table shows the health of each node, its requests over the last hour, its mesh link and its certificate. The health is healthy, warning, failing or unknown. Under the health, the table names the step of a job that runs, for example "writing and starting the stack (2 of 3)". Without a job, it names the check that fails, or it shows the count of differences from the config. All and Problems filter the table. During an update, a strip above the table shows the part of each node in the rollout.

Select a node to open it in the Inspector. The Inspector has these sections:

  • Checks, with the checks that fail at the top. See Node checks.
  • The charts: Requests served, Egress to visitors, Mesh link in, homelab to node and Mesh link out, node to homelab.
  • Differences from config, when HomeGAP found drift.
  • System: the address, the management name, the provider, the system facts and the software version.
  • Runs: the last 10 runs of provisioning and updates.

The actions on a node are Re-provision, Pause or Resume, Diagnostics, Speed test, Terminal, Change location and Remove. Change location moves the node to a known city or a point on the map. Geo DNS and the maps use the new place from the next pass. After a removal, the action is Decommission. After a failed update, the node also has Retry update and Skip update. See Manage nodes and Node updates and rollback.

+ Add node opens the wizard over the page. When a run fails, Retry runs each step again. If something blocked the new SSH connections of the orchestrator, the button shows a time, for example "Retry in 2:59". See Add a node.

The Mesh panel is below the table. For each pair of members, it shows the time of the last WireGuard handshake. A link in use makes a handshake approximately every 2 minutes. See Mesh.

items.title: Services
items.text:
The page shows each service, with its response time through each node. Amber is slow (over 1 s). Rose is failing, with the status code. A dash means that the node does not serve it.

The health of a service through a node has two parts. The first part is the mesh link of the node. The second part is one HTTPS request through the Traefik of the node, on each pass. HomeGAP sends the request only for public HTTP services, and the request accepts each certificate. No answer in 3 seconds or a 5xx status is a failure.

Filter by hostname or container. Select a service to see how each node serves it, how HomeGAP publishes it and its source labels. Each service has Pause service or Resume service, and Logs, which opens the Diagnostics page. An http or https service also has Open.

items.title: DNS
items.text:
The page shows the records that HomeGAP manages, grouped into record sets. A healthy record set shows as one line. A record set with a problem also shows each member, with its monitor and its state. Filter by name or value. A plain record is in sync only when each nameserver of the zone serves it. The geo steering strip shows which nodes answer now and which are withdrawn, and for how long.

The CAA record sets belong to certificate management. They are read-only, and they link to the Certificates tab.

With extra domains, the page also has the Domains table. It shows each domain with its DNS zone, its front door and its state.

items.title: Zone records
items.text:
The Zone records tab of the DNS page shows every record of one DNS zone. A record that HomeGAP manages has a lock and shows what it is for. You cannot change a locked record.

Each other record is yours. Click Add record to add one, or click a record to edit or delete it. A typical use is a TXT record that a service needs to check your domain. See DNS routing and health checks.

items.title: Certificates
items.text: A tab of the DNS page. It shows the certificate that the nodes share, which node has it, what a visitor gets on each name through each node, and the orders. See Certificates.

items.title: Access
items.text:
The page shows who can sign in to the apps, and their devices. + Add user and + Add machine are in the head of the page. The App address panel has the address for the Pangolin apps, with Copy and Show QR. Select a person to change their roles, then click Save. A person also has New password, Block or Unblock, and Remove. A device has Block or Unblock, and Delete.

Without sign_in.url in the config, the page shows "Access isn't available right now.". See Users, machines and devices.

items.title: Speed test
items.text: The page measures the latency and the throughput through the real traffic path. Test all nodes tests each node in turn on the orchestrator, so the run continues when you close the page. See Speed tests.

items.title: Activity
items.text: The page shows the reconcile log, with the newest entry first. Passes that change nothing show as one row with their count. Filter by level, domain or text. Each entry belongs to a numbered pass. Select an entry to see its details, and click Show pass #N to see only that pass. Load older gets older entries. The orchestrator keeps the last 10,000 entries in its data directory, so the log continues after a restart.

items.title: Diagnostics
items.text: The page shows container logs and a read-only snapshot of each node. See Diagnostics and troubleshooting.

items.title: Config
items.text:
The page shows:

  • Differences: the differences between the desired state and the actual state.
  • Secrets: each secret that the config names, as present or missing. The page never shows the values.
  • Desired state and Config file. Each opens when you select it, and each has Copy.

Locations in the head of the page opens the Locations page over it. See Maps and locations.

items.title: Terminal
items.text:
The dashboard can open a shell on a node. The Terminal action is in the menu of a node on the Nodes page and in the Inspector of the node. The terminal opens in a panel at the bottom of the dashboard, and the panel stays open when you go to a different page.

The shell runs through the SSH connection that the orchestrator already has to the node. The browser gets no key and no password. You are the management user of the node.

  • Each session has a tab. You can have 2 sessions for one node and 6 sessions in total.
  • A session continues when you close or reload the page. When you open the dashboard again, the tab is there.
  • If you open the same session in a second window, that window takes the session.
  • Commands types a common command for you, for example the list of containers or the log of Traefik.
  • A session ends when the shell exits, or when you close its tab. HomeGAP also ends a session that had no browser for 15 minutes, and each session after 8 hours.

The activity log shows when a terminal opens and closes, with the node. It does not record what you type or what the shell prints.

Warning

A terminal gives a shell on the node to each person who has the dashboard token. To disable the terminal, set dashboard.terminal: false.

items.title: Node checks
items.text:
The Inspector of a node shows these checks:

Check Name on the dashboard What it shows ssh SSH If the orchestrator can reach the node over SSH. docker Docker If Docker is on the node, with its version. traefik Traefik The state of the container: running, with its Docker health in parentheses. A container that does not run is a failure. homegap-maintenance Maintenance page The state of the container of the maintenance page. homegap-agent HomeGAP agent The state of the container of the agent. tls-mgmt Management certificate The certificate that the node serves for its management name, with the days that remain. No certificate is a failure. The certificate that HomeGAP renews is a warning when its renewal is late. A different certificate is a warning with fewer than 14 days. tls-root Root name TLS The certificate that the node serves for the root name. mesh Mesh link If the homelab and the node had a WireGuard handshake in the last 200 seconds. mode In dry run, it shows that HomeGAP does no remote access.

items.title: Banners
items.text:
The dashboard shows a banner in these cases:

  • HomeGAP runs in dry-run mode.
  • Changes are paused. The banner has Resume.
  • A node update fails and holds the rollout. The banner has Retry and Skip for the node. See Node updates and rollback.
  • The config has two or more nodes, and none of them answers over SSH. The banner tells you that the homelab cannot reach a node. The nodes continue to serve. After the homelab reaches a node again, a banner tells you how long the loss was. That banner stays for one hour.
  • The orchestrator answers requests but refuses the event stream. The banner starts with "No live updates".

items.title: Documentation
items.text: The Documentation link at the bottom of the menu opens these docs at /docs/, for the version that runs.

items.title: Failure modes
items.text: This page tells you what happens when a part of the system fails, and how to recover. The orchestrator is never in the traffic path. Thus a failure of the orchestrator does not affect live traffic.

items.title: The homelab, a node and the mesh
items.text: Failure Effect Recovery A node is down. Bunny removes the node from DNS when its health check fails. Its viewers resolve to a different node. The orchestrator repairs the node or provisions it again. DNS recovers by itself. The mesh link of one node is down. That node cannot reach the homelab. Its mesh check fails, and the services through it fail. A site that the node terminates shows the "back shortly" page. The health check of Bunny fails for the node, so Bunny removes it from DNS. The other nodes continue to serve. Repair the network. WireGuard connects again by itself. Make sure that mesh.port/udp is open on the node. The homelab is down, or it has no internet connection. Public services are down, because the homelab is the single origin. See When the homelab is down. Restore the homelab. The mesh links connect again by themselves. The orchestrator is down. Live traffic does not change. New label changes and config changes wait. The dashboard is not available. Start the orchestrator again. It reconciles to the desired state. The homelab restarts, and the orchestrator starts before the app containers. HomeGAP keeps the services of each container that is gone for reconcile.removal_grace (default 3 minutes). The containers start, and nothing changes. The homelab cannot reach a node over SSH, but the nodes serve. With two or more nodes, and no answer from any of them, the dashboard shows a banner. Provisioning and the node checks wait. Check the internet connection of the homelab. See Manage nodes.

items.title: When the homelab is down
items.text:
The maintenance service on each node checks every 2 seconds that the homelab answers over the mesh. After three checks with no answer, the node changes what it serves. This takes approximately 15 seconds.

Traffic What the node does A site that the node terminates It shows a "back shortly" page with status 503. The label homegap.maintenance_page: "false" disables the page for a service. A passthrough site It closes the connection immediately. The node has no certificate for the name, so it cannot show a page. A raw TCP or UDP port The connection fails. The status page and the speed test The node shows the "back shortly" page.

When the homelab answers two checks in a row, the node removes the page.

The sign-in and the VPN change as follows:

  • A node answers the sign-in address itself. The Traefik of each node checks the sign-in of the homelab every 5 seconds, and uses the agent of the node when that check fails.
  • A user can sign in at a node with a HomeGAP password. The OpenID Connect provider is not available at a node. With sign_in.passwords: false, no user can sign in during the outage. A machine can.
  • A device that signs in at a node gets the exits only. "Exit via <node>" continues to work. Private services of the homelab and "Exit via homelab" do not work.
  • A block of a user or a device does not reach a node until the homelab is up again.
  • The homelab does not know a device that a node created. After the outage, the user of that device signs in again.

See Connect the Pangolin apps.

items.title: The sign-in
items.text: Failure Effect Recovery The homegap-sign-in container is down, and the homelab is up. The nodes answer the sign-in address themselves, as during an outage of the homelab. A new sign-in gets the exits only. Public services continue to work. Start the container: docker compose up -d homegap-sign-in. The OpenID Connect provider is down. A sign-in through the provider fails. A sign-in with a HomeGAP password works, unless sign_in.passwords is false. Restore the provider. The config has no sign_in.url. There is no sign-in and no VPN. The Access page is not available. Set sign_in.url. See Sign-in.

items.title: Updates and removal
items.text: Failure Effect Recovery A node update fails. HomeGAP rolls that node back to its previous stack. The rollout to the other nodes stops. Click Retry update or Skip update, or change the config. See Node updates and rollback. The first provisioning of a node fails. The node gets no DNS records. HomeGAP tries again after 5 minutes. To try immediately, click Re-provision. The teardown of a removed node fails. The node stays on the Nodes page as teardown failed. Its stack can still run. Decommission the node again, or forget it. See Manage nodes. The upgrade of the homelab fails at the orchestrator. upgrade.sh restores the previous image of the orchestrator and stops. Read the log of the orchestrator. See Upgrade the homelab.

items.title: DNS and certificates
items.text: Failure Effect Recovery Bunny has an outage. DNS resolution has problems. None. Bunny is the single external dependency of the traffic path. A new record is not on every Bunny nameserver. The DNS page shows the record as not in sync. HomeGAP checks again on every pass. If the record does not arrive, save it again in the Bunny dashboard. The order of the certificate of the nodes fails. The nodes keep the certificate that they have. A node without one serves a default certificate, so a browser shows a warning for the names that the node terminates. The Certificates tab of the DNS page shows the cause. See Certificates.

items.title: Access to the nodes
items.text: Failure Effect Recovery A login blocker on a node (fail2ban, sshguard or CrowdSec) bans the orchestrator. SSH from the orchestrator times out, or the server cuts it before login. Setup or provisioning for that node fails. Remove the ban from the console of the provider or from a different network. Then try again. The IP address of the orchestrator changes, and the config has ssh_allow_from. Provisioning and the SSH checks fail for those nodes. Live traffic does not change. Open SSH again from the console of the provider (ufw allow <port>/tcp). Then update ssh_allow_from.

items.title: The state of the orchestrator
items.text: Failure Effect Recovery The file state.json in the data directory is gone. The orchestrator starts from an empty state. It loses the pauses, the update holds and the slot of each node. Restore the file from a backup of the data directory. The file state.json is there, but HomeGAP cannot read it. HomeGAP uses state.json.bak, the copy from its last start. It keeps the damaged file as state.json.corrupt. Without a good copy, the orchestrator does not start. Live traffic does not change. Restore state.json from a backup. To start from an empty state, delete the file.

items.title: Maps and locations
items.text: The dashboard and the public status page have maps of your nodes and your homelab. This page tells you what the maps show and how to set locations.

items.title: Where the maps are
items.text:
These pages have a world map that you can drag and zoom:

  • The Overview, Speed test and Locations pages.
  • The add-node wizard and the Change location dialog of a node.
  • The public status page.

The maps get nothing from a third party. The orchestrator serves all parts:

  • The map library (MapLibre GL).
  • The styles (Protomaps).
  • The fonts and the icons.
  • The map data from OpenStreetMap, as one PMTiles file of approximately 45 MB, to zoom level 6. This is sufficient for cities and regions.

The release image includes the tiles.

items.title: The Overview map
items.text:
On the Overview page, select Map in the Network panel. The map shows every node and the homelab as markers in their health color. Lines go from the homelab to each node, in the color of its mesh link. The homelab marker and the lines show only after you set the location of the homelab. A node with a region but no location is at the center of its region, marked "(approximate)". A node with neither has no marker.

When you move the pointer over a node, the map shows details of the node. These are its health, its mesh link, its provider, its failed checks and the time of its last provisioning. The details of the homelab show how many mesh links are up.

items.title: The other maps
items.text:
On the Speed test map, each line has the latest result between the homelab and the node. Click a node to run its test.

In the add-node wizard, search the known data-center cities, for example "dallas", "london" or "hetzner". The search gives the place name, the region code and the coordinates. Or click the map: the nearest known city within 50 km gives the point its name.

The Change location action of a node uses the same search. Geo DNS and the maps use the new place from the next pass. The API call is PUT /api/nodes/{id}/location.

items.title: The Locations page
items.text:
To open the Locations page, click Locations in the head of the Config page. It has two parts.

The Homelab part tells the maps where the homelab is. Search a city or click the map, then click Save homelab location. You can also set homelab.location in the config. The API call is PUT /api/homelab/location. The public status page shows only the region of the homelab.

The Known locations part is the catalog. Approximately 100 data-center cities come with HomeGAP, with the providers in each city. You can add your own locations, and edit or remove the locations that come with HomeGAP. The Source column shows shipped, edited or added. HomeGAP keeps your changes in <data_dir>/locations.yml.

items.title: Custom tiles
items.text: To build tiles with more detail, run tools/build-map.sh tiles from the repository, with MAP_MAXZOOM set to a higher zoom level. The script builds the tiles from a Protomaps build. Then set map.tiles to the path of the bigger file. The default path is /usr/share/homegap/map/world.pmtiles.

items.title: Attribution
items.text: Map data © OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL), through Protomaps.

items.title: Node updates and rollback
items.text: HomeGAP updates the stacks of the nodes one at a time, and it rolls back a failed update. This page tells you how an update works and how to recover from a failure.

items.title: Provisioning in the background
items.text:
Provisioning runs in the background. A slow node never delays the health checks, the mesh or DNS for the other nodes. Examples of a slow node are a first install or a slow Docker download.

During provisioning, the Nodes page shows the current phase of the node, for example writing and starting the stack (2 of 3). The phases are:

  1. preparing the host: the preflight checks, Docker, the firewall and the TCP tuning.
  2. backing up the stack: only for an update.
  3. writing and starting the stack: HomeGAP writes the files and runs docker compose up -d. Then it waits up to 2 minutes for Traefik to answer.
  4. verifying: the containers traefik, homegap-maintenance and homegap-agent must run, and a process must listen on port 443.

items.title: A rolling update
items.text:
Some changes alter the stack of nodes that are already healthy. Examples are a new image version, node_stack.crowdsec and node_stack.tcp_tuning. HomeGAP sends such a change to one node at a time:

  1. HomeGAP saves the stack that runs on the node, in <install_dir>/.homegap-rollback. The copy has compose.yml, .env and the config folder. It does not have the logs of Traefik or the data of CrowdSec.
  2. HomeGAP updates the node. The node must then pass the verifying phase.
  3. If a step fails, HomeGAP restores the saved stack and starts it again. The node continues to serve on the old stack.

After an update that succeeds, HomeGAP removes the Docker images that no container on the node uses.

The routes of the services, the spec of the agent and the certificate are not a part of the stack. HomeGAP writes them to a node when they change, with no rollout. No container starts again for them.

items.title: A failed update
items.text:
A failed update holds the rollout. HomeGAP does not update other nodes, and the dashboard shows the banner "Update rollout held." with the node. To recover, do one of these actions:

  • Correct the cause on the node. Then click Retry update. HomeGAP applies the update to that node again.
  • Click Skip update. The node stays on its current stack, and the rollout continues with the other nodes.
  • Change the config. HomeGAP tries the new desired stack on the failed node first, and then on the other nodes. If you revert the change, the failure clears.

The API calls are POST /api/nodes/{id}/update/retry and POST /api/nodes/{id}/update/skip.

If the rollback also fails, the Nodes page shows the node with update failed and the provisioning error. Correct the cause on the node. Then click Retry update.

items.title: What does not wait
items.text:
New nodes and drift repairs do not wait for a rollout.

If the first provisioning of a node fails, HomeGAP tries again after 5 minutes. To try again immediately, click Re-provision.

The steps on the host (Docker, the firewall and the TCP tuning) are idempotent. HomeGAP does not roll them back.

items.title: Drift
items.text: Every reconcile.node_check_interval (default 5 minutes), HomeGAP checks each node over SSH. It compares each file of the stack with the file that it wrote, and it checks that the three containers run. It repairs the changes that somebody makes outside HomeGAP. To keep a change that you make by hand, pause the node. See Manage nodes.

items.title: Preview the stack of a node
items.text:
To see the stack that HomeGAP writes to a node, run this command. The output does not show the secrets. It reads only the config file, so it has no services from labels.

docker compose exec orchestrator homegap render-node na1

items.title: Move the SSH port of a node
items.text:
To move the SSH server of a node to a different port, change nodes[].ssh_port in the config. HomeGAP moves the server in the next pass. A reason to do this is a service that needs port 22 on the nodes. See Raw TCP and UDP ports.

HomeGAP keeps a way in at each step:

  1. Over the old port, it makes the SSH server listen on the old port and on the new port. It opens the new port in the firewall.
  2. It connects on the new port.
  3. Over the new port, it makes the SSH server drop the old port. The firewall closes the old port in the same pass.

If the connection on the new port fails, HomeGAP restores the old ports. The activity log has the error "the SSH port stays N", and HomeGAP tries the move again in each pass. Until the move is complete, HomeGAP uses the old port for the node. A cause of a failed connection is a firewall of your provider that does not have the new port open.

HomeGAP does not move the port during a dry run, a pause of all changes or a pause of the node.

The ports are in the file /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-homegap-port.conf on the node.

Caution

Keep the console of your provider ready for the first move of a node. It is the way in if the SSH server and HomeGAP disagree about the port.

items.title: Manage nodes
items.text: This page tells you how to add, remove, re-provision and pause nodes, and how to work on a node by hand.

items.title: Add a node
items.text:
Use the add-node wizard, or add an entry to nodes[] in the config. HomeGAP provisions the node on the next pass. It adds the node to DNS only after the stack of the node is up. See Add a node.

The API call is POST /api/nodes. It adds the node to the config file.

items.title: Remove a node
items.text:
A removal has two parts. First you remove the node from the config, and its DNS records drain. Then you decommission the node, and HomeGAP removes its stack from the server.

  1. Click Remove on the Nodes page. Or remove the node from nodes[] in the config file. The DNS records of the node drain on the next pass.
  2. Make sure that the node has the status pending decommission. Its stack continues to run.
  3. Click Decommission.
  4. Type the node id to confirm.

The API calls are DELETE /api/nodes/{id} and POST /api/nodes/{id}/decommission?confirm={id}.

Until the decommission, you can undo the removal. The dashboard offers Undo for 30 seconds. After that, add the node to the config again with the same id. The node stays in the mesh until the decommission, so it needs no new setup.

The decommission does these steps on the node:

  1. It stops the stack and removes its containers and volumes.
  2. It removes the exit interface (hg-exit) and the mesh interface (hg-mesh).
  3. It removes the install directory, with the data and the secrets of the stack.

Then HomeGAP removes the node from its state. The server itself continues to run. Delete it at your provider. If you add the node again, it starts as a new node.

Warning

A decommission deletes the install directory of the node (/opt/homegap by default). You cannot undo it.

items.title: If the teardown fails
items.text:
If HomeGAP cannot connect to the node, or a step of the teardown fails, the node stays on the Nodes page with the status teardown failed. The activity log shows the error. The stack and the secrets of the node can still be on the server.

  • To try again, click Decommission again.
  • If the server is gone, click Forget node. HomeGAP then removes the node from its list and does not connect to the server. The API call is POST /api/nodes/{id}/decommission?confirm={id}&force=true.

Warning

Forget node leaves the stack and the secrets on a server that still runs. Use it only after you delete the server at the provider.

items.title: Re-provision a node
items.text:
Click Re-provision on the Nodes page. HomeGAP runs each provisioning step again: it writes the stack and restarts the containers whose files changed. The node continues to serve during the run. The API call is POST /api/nodes/{id}/provision.

HomeGAP can build each node again from an empty server, so you can destroy and recreate a VPS. A rebuilt server has a new host key. In the wizard, click Forget the old host key and retry.

items.title: Pause
items.text:
You can pause at three levels:

  • Everything, with Pause all at the bottom of the menu.
  • One node, with Pause on the Nodes page.
  • One service, with Pause service on the Services page, or with the label homegap.pause.

The dashboard asks you to confirm each pause. A resume needs no confirmation.

Level What HomeGAP does during the pause Everything It only observes. It applies nothing to the nodes, DNS or the mesh. A node It does not provision the node and does not repair its drift. Config changes and updates for the node wait. A service It holds the DNS records of the service. The routes of the service stay on the nodes.

The API call is POST /api/pause with a body like this:

{"scope": "node", "id": "na1", "paused": true}

The scope is global, node or service.

items.title: The management name
items.text: Each node has a management name, node-<id>.<domain> by default. To use a different name, set nodes[].management_host. The name has its own plain DNS record, with the address of that node only. The name is on the certificate of the nodes, and the tls-mgmt check reads the certificate that the node serves for it.

items.title: Work on a node by hand
items.text:
The stack is in /opt/homegap (node_stack.install_dir). To open a shell there, use the Terminal action of the node. See The dashboard.

Caution

A change that you make by hand is drift. HomeGAP repairs it on the next node check. To keep the change, pause the node first.

items.title: When the homelab loses every node
items.text:
If the config has two or more nodes and none of them answers over SSH, the dashboard shows a banner. The activity log records the start and the end. The nodes continue to serve.

Two providers rarely fail at the same moment, so the first thing to check is the internet connection of the homelab. If the Mesh panel shows handshakes between the nodes during the outage, the problem was the connection of the homelab. See Failure modes.

items.title: Node slots
items.text: Each node gets a permanent slot, which the orchestrator keeps in its state. The slot gives the node its mesh address and its exit address. A new node takes the lowest free slot. A removal or a new order of nodes never moves a different node. HomeGAP has 32 slots, so 32 nodes is the limit. See Mesh.

items.title: Performance
items.text: This page tells you which parts of the traffic path set the throughput, and what HomeGAP does to keep it high.

items.title: The path of a request
items.text:
A web request crosses two TCP connections. The first one is from the viewer to the Traefik of the node. The second one is from that Traefik to the container on the homelab, over the WireGuard mesh. The mesh namespace of the homelab forwards the packets of the second connection. It does not end the connection.

A raw TCP or UDP port has no second connection. The kernel of the node forwards its packets over the mesh. A port with the PROXY protocol goes through the agent of the node.

items.title: TCP tuning on the nodes
items.text:
With node_stack.tcp_tuning: true (the default), HomeGAP writes /etc/sysctl.d/99-homegap.conf on each node and applies it. The file has these settings:

Setting Value Effect net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control bbr BBR keeps the throughput high on a long path with packet loss. net.core.default_qdisc fq BBR uses fq to pace the packets. net.core.rmem_max, net.core.wmem_max 64 MiB The largest socket buffers. net.ipv4.tcp_rmem, net.ipv4.tcp_wmem Up to 64 MiB The TCP windows can grow to the size that a fast, long path needs. net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing 1 TCP finds a packet size that works when path MTU discovery fails across the mesh. net.ipv4.tcp_slow_start_after_idle 0 A connection keeps its window after an idle time. net.ipv4.tcp_reordering, net.ipv4.tcp_max_reordering 10, 1000 Long routes often reorder packets. TCP then does not read that as loss.

A container does not get the TCP settings of the host. Thus HomeGAP also sets the buffers, the MTU probing, the slow start and the reordering values on the Traefik container of the node. Each connection from a node to a viewer and to the homelab starts in that container.

HomeGAP does not change the TCP settings of the containers on the homelab.

items.title: Check the result
items.text:
Some VPS kernels refuse BBR or other settings. HomeGAP then writes the warning "some TCP tuning sysctls could not be applied" to the activity log.

The node keeps three facts, which GET /api/status shows:

Fact What it shows tcp_cc The congestion control that the kernel of the node uses. qdisc The default qdisc of the node. edge_tcp The congestion control and the largest send buffer in the Traefik container, for example bbr 64MiB.

The Inspector of a node shows tcp_cc and qdisc in the TCP row.

items.title: Disable the tuning
items.text: Set node_stack.tcp_tuning: false. HomeGAP then removes the file from the node and the settings from the Traefik container. The values of the host stay until the next restart of the node. The change is a stack update, so it goes to one node at a time.

items.title: VPN traffic
items.text:
The traffic of a VPN device always goes through a node. The device sends its WireGuard packets to a node on vpn.port, and the node forwards them to the homelab over the mesh. There is no direct path from a device to the homelab. Thus the rate of a device has two limits: the path from the device to the node, and the path from the node to the homelab.

With "Exit via <node>", the traffic leaves for the internet from that node and does not go to the homelab. See Exits and tunnel DNS.

items.title: Measure the result
items.text: To measure the throughput through the real path, use the speed tests. The test between the homelab and a node also shows the CPU load of the two machines. Thus you can see if a CPU or the network is the limit. See Speed tests.

items.title: Speed tests
items.text: The speed tests measure the latency and the throughput through the real traffic path. This page tells you how to enable them and what each test measures.

items.title: Enable the speed tests
items.text:
With speedtest.enabled: true, the orchestrator serves a speed test origin on speedtest.bind. The speed tests need a front door.

Key Default What it does speedtest.enabled false Enables the speed tests. speedtest.hostname speedtest The first label of the names of the speed test. speedtest.bind 0.0.0.0:8089 The listener of the speed test origin. The status page uses it too. speedtest.link_ttl 2h The lifetime of a test link. speedtest.phase_seconds 8 The length of the download phase and of the upload phase, from 2 to 30. speedtest.link_budget_gb 20 The data that one test link can send and receive, in GiB. speedtest.vpn_access false Lets a VPN device open the page with no link. speedtest.streams 4 The parallel streams of a test between the homelab and a node, from 1 to 16.

The speed test and the status page share one listener, which starts only with the orchestrator. If neither was on at the start, the first activation needs a restart of the orchestrator. A change of speedtest.bind also needs a restart.
